utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Mr. Brdjanin is here. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours, this is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Brdjanin, good morning to you and the usual question. Can you follow in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Julian Nicholls with Joanna Korner and Denise Gustin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you. Appearances for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. David Cunningham with Barbara Baruch and Vesna Anic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you, too. Any preliminaries? No? Let's bring the witness in. Just for the record, Madam Registrar, would you just announce the time schedule for today, what time we will be sitting? We have started at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We start at 9.00 and then we going to have a break at 10.30 and we're going to resume at 11.00 and then going to have a break at 12.30, and then have a lunch break from 12.30 to 2.00 and then we're going to sit from 2.00 to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I want to mention something in relation to the length of time I have for this witness but I'll wait until -- for the next witness. I'll wait until this witness is finished.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just to make it clear, we are flexible, I mean, if you want to start at 2.30 instead of 2.00 and finish at 4.30 instead of 4.00, we are flexible. It's not something which needs to be strictly adhered to.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome. You won't be here for long, I hope but we still require from you that you repeat the solemn declaration that you made yesterday and the day before. Usher, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. You may sit down. Please be seated. Mrs. Baruch.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: May it please the Court, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Mr. Mujanic, good morning.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I have one more question about the German statement that you gave at Kirhajm Tek. Can you tell me what year you gave that statement? Was it when you just arrived in the Stuttgart area?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in 1996, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Do you remember the month?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you the exact date, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Not even the month? Okay.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Mr. Mujanic, do you know Zaim Zukandzic?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Are you related to him?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. He is my brother-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. And did he visit you at Sloga?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Once he did.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Did he bring you food at the Dom Kulture?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Also once.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: And did he bring you blankets at Sloga?

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Can you tell me, then, why he might say something like, "While in Lisnja, we learned that many of the men from Lisnja who were detained at the Sloga factory and Dom Kulture were not being fed. Myself and others were allowed to go to these camps to visit our relatives. I went to visit my relatives, Sead Carkaric [phoen], Zulfo Zukandzic, Muharem Zuric [phoen], and Rusmir Mujanic. I was allowed to bring food to my relatives and after the men were taken to Sloga, I would also visit them and bring food. They had no blankets and we also brought them blankets as well."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where are you reading from, please, Madam Baruch?

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: It's from a statement I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It may be regular in Texas.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I should have stood up I know it's Mr. Nicholls' witness, but as you know Your Honour I've raised this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we have raised it before and it's a --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's not in our submission proper, it's even less proper now from a statement to put to a witness what another witness may have said in a statement and may have said in court. It is of course perfectly proper to ask the witness whether he agrees with something without indicating what it is or where it comes from.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I tried not to indicate where it came from but may I pose the question differently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's too late now. You didn't -- I don't agree with you at all when you say that you tried not to indicate where it came from, because your previous question was precisely this: Can you tell me, then, why he might say something like -- and then you started reading. Then I asked you where you were reading from, and you said it's from a statement that I have. This kind of incident has happened before, with Mr. Ackerman, and the practice here is that it is not regular. You can address a question to the witness without indicating who the maker of the statement is or who may have stated that. You put the question whether it's correct or not, and he will answer that, but it's not regular -- I mean it's not a practice that is accepted by this Trial Chamber. Or by other Trial Chambers for that matter.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Would then it be proper, Your Honour, for me to ask why would a person without saying their name indicate that they had brought him a blanket.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, you just put the question to him, which you did already, whether his relative, Mr. so and so did bring him.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Blankets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He answered in the negative. And it should stop there. Then later on, if you need to bring forward evidence to contradict what the witness has stated, you're free to do that but you don't confront the witness with the statement made by someone else here in -- during -- in the course of his testimony. That's the practice of this Court.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: The thing that had confused me is I was told --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're new here so I'm not blaming you I'm just explaining to you what the practice is.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I thought one had to put it to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You put it already. You had put it already.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: Okay. I don't know how to proceed, then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I think you have to forget it now and move to the next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I have no next question, Your Honour. That's the end of my questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. BARUCH
utterances.text: I suppose I have to pass the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Are you sure, Mr. Mujanic, that you never received any blankets from anyone while you were at Sloga?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sure that I did not receive any blankets from anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So Ms. Korner -- sorry, Mr. Nicholls, is there re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Judge Janu? Yes, Judge Janu would like to put some questions to you, Mr. Mujanic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, I would like to take you back to your testimony, when you were describing for us the establishment of the TO, and you said that there was some sort of order for you to choose the group of people and you did so, you chose -- you were not -- 40 or 48 people, and you also said that you have chosen those who were free of alcohol and you have chosen calm people. I would like to know if this condition, so say, to choose secure people, was a part of the order you received or if it was your consideration that the people who cannot be trusted cannot have a gun for free use. So my question is if it was part of the order, these conditions, or if it was just your natural consideration.

utterances.speaker: RUSMIR MUJANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was our natural reaction because people who are prone to drinking, they can do all sorts of things if they are drunk. They can provoke people or hurt somebody. So that's what we did amongst ourselves in the village. We chose those people that we considered would be appropriate for the task. So that would be that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Thank you. That's all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't have any questions either, which essentially means that your testimony ends here. On behalf of the Tribunal and on behalf of my two colleagues and my own behalf I should like to thank you for having come over to give evidence, to testify in this case. You will be attended to by the usher first and later on by other officers of this Tribunal to ensure that you will be able to return to your country and they will attend to all your needs in the meantime. Once more I thank you and you're free to go now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you and goodbye.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Safe journey.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would now tender the Prnjavor binder which has been provided, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. With the numbers that -- consecutive numbers as they appear in each of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Are you happy with that, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. You don't have any reason to ask questions or clarification? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know if I should also mention the three new exhibits which I put in with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think they have been admitted already.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: That's what I thought. I just wanted to make sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The thing is this: That --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner yesterday in our oral decision, we did point out three or four documents that you need to bring Mr. Inayat or whoever, I don't know who.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I put Mr. Inayat back on to this problem. As Your Honour knows, there are various forms that are completed to show where exhibits come from. These particular forms for some reason only indicate who received them and not from where. And Mr. Inayat is making attempts to see if we can expand on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If not, I think we may be able to deal with them through another route, but that's a matter for the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But Your Honour may I deal with the exhibits previous exhibits? Because I've been helpfully -- we have been helpfully reminded by the Registrar that we haven't yet actually formally moved into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The binders which related to Bosanski Novi, Donji Vakuf and the five or so from Prijedor. Your Honour, I may be wrong but I don't recall any objection from the Defence to any of the documents, and it's one of the matters I raised the day before yesterday in those binders, and I would therefore ask Your Honours formally to admit them into evidence, the documents contained therein, subject to the usual caveat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So the Chamber reserves its decision on this, after Mrs. Baruch or Mr. Cunningham will confer with Mr. Ackerman and in the meantime everyone can check. After that we can easily decide yes or no or 100 per cent or less than 100 per cent. But it's something that can be looked into. But please on Monday, Mrs. Baruch, please come back with some kind of response. If not directly to us, through the Registrar, you can communicate Mr. Ackerman's response to Ms. Korner or the -- someone else from the team, the Prosecution team, and we will attend to it then on Monday, first thing. Okay? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I come back then to today's witness for two matters?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment until I find where -- okay. They are all here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As Your Honour is aware, I think, the witness arrived the day before yesterday, bringing with him a bundle of further documents which we had translated at speed over night and I'm deeply grateful and I think it's worth mentioning to Your Honours it was not done by CLSS but by persons in another unit whose normal job is not to do translations and they literally worked I think all night. They haven't, however, been done by CLSS. Therefore, they are not in that sense authorised translations, so if there are errors, Your Honour, I hope that Your Honour will forgive it and if it turns out that there are serious errors, then we will try and correct it. Your Honour, I should also say the documents themselves with three exceptions are in fact the -- I'll come back to what I mean by originals but they are the originals that he copied, if Your Honours saw attached to his statement was his own notebook, and he'd copied various documents that he was given and he'll explain how he came by them when he testifies. These are the actual documents themselves. He has with him the originals of the documents he has acquired, and by originals, I understand, though I haven't seen them myself, they are not photocopies, they are actual -- it's so long since typewriters were used, carbon copies which he was provided with so I asked him when I spoke with him yesterday to bring them with him today so that Your Honours and the Defence can look at them if they so require. Your Honour, that's the first point. As I say, there are only three which have not in some form or other been notified to the Defence. Your Honour, the second matter is this: I heard Your Honours' discussion yesterday with Mr. Nicholls about the time that I have to call him. Your Honours, the problem -- I go back to what I said the day before yesterday, Mr. Ackerman has raised an objection to every document in this binder, bar two. In order therefore really to, as it were, persuade Your Honours that these are documents that are probative, Your Honours, I would have to establish through evidence that what is said in them is correct or that they had been seen before or where they came from. Now this witness can actually assist with quite a lot of them. Your Honours, I don't want to take any more time than I have to over this and that is why I asked whether or not Mr. Ackerman might rethink what is effectively in our submission a sweeping and not particularly selective objection. Some I can see like the ones Your Honours have ruled we have to find other evidence but Your Honour, I'm asking Your Honours, I will try and finish today with this witness in chief, but if I have to take him through and establish to Your Honour's satisfaction that these documents are authentic, and did come into existence when we suggest that they did, well, then, Your Honours, it means taking him to many of the documents so Your Honour that's the application I make and the only thing I really would like to know from Your Honours today or now is whether Your Honours will restrict me just to today in chief. That's the only question I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We haven't discussed this. Ideally, yes, if it is possible to finish today, it would be ideal, and with the understanding that the same thing will be done with the Defence. In other words, the thing is Ms. Korner let's proceed and then we will decide as we go along, because if you consider this to be a key witness, particularly with regard to the authenticity and probative value of some documents, you have been working with us for long enough to know that we do not try to shut you down or to restrict your --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What I may try to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or the Defence for that matter, if it's -- we only clamp down on you when it's necessary.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think Your Honour is going to hear an answer from some of the documents he brought which as Your Honour will hear have never been supplied to AID and Your Honour will see that their identical to the ones supplied in the format and the like. Your Honour what I may try and do, subject to any objection by the Defence, is I'm dealing with this evidence by topics and there are many documents that relates to topics and I may say -- ask him to look at a couple and then simply mention the exhibit numbers that also relate to the same topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps what you could also do, Ms. Korner, is to gather these documents that you are mostly interested in, in a bundle, and we will hand them over to the witness and then perhaps you could use a blanket formula in the kind of questions that you ask him with reference to all those documents in general, plus, if he has anything to add with regard to any one of them in particular, and we tried -- we tried to cover the question of authenticity in that manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think if Your Honours simply -- it's easier if it stays because the Petrovac bundle is chronological, the documents slot in that way. I will simply refer him to the documents that I consider --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I want to make sure and it's my duty to make sure is that when he is asked questions about documents in general and particular, he knows exactly which documents he's being asked about.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's very important for me. I mean, it's more important for me to stop and wait until he goes through all these documents to make sure that he knows what he's talking about rather than to go through some other procedure lengthy or shorter but I mean it's up to you. I do not --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand. Your Honour, for reasons that are obvious because we are stacked up with witnesses next week, I would like to be able to finish him in any event today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course, Mrs. Baruch, you will have every opportunity to cross-examine, Mr. Cunningham you'll have every opportunity to cross-examine the witness on any of these documents. I mean this is something that if I may add, since both of you are new to this case, this is something that arose in the early stages of the trial, especially when the French team of lawyers defending General Talic were present. They had come forward with a sort of a generic, blanket objection to all documents coming from a specific source. Mr. Ackerman was less generic than them, and he restricted his objection to documents, to the exhibiting of, tendering of documents in exhibit to certain documents only. In the course of the proceedings here, one of these sources which Mr. Ackerman generally contests is the AID. So his objection is in line with what he has been doing until now. The understanding, however, has also been in the sense that source is -- attendability of the source is not something that is pre-emptively decided before the trial starts or in the early stages of the trial. It's something that we will consider as we go along and we'll decide upon at the right time, together with all the other evidence, because it may well be that a document which has been furnished by AID to the Prosecution, Office of the Prosecutor, is also -- exists also in other places and as is most often the case is also produced by witnesses or brought forward by witnesses, et cetera. So you will convey this to Mr. Ackerman at your earliest and in the meantime we proceed and you regulate the way you conduct -- I mean that's something in which we will not interfere.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The next witness does not have any protective measures.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just because, Mr. Cunningham, I haven't looked upon him before, I propose, unless there is an objection, to lead on background matters and irrelevant matters because otherwise we will take a long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think there shouldn't be an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I don't have any objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Usher? Could you please bring in the next witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Welcome to this Tribunal. I take it from the way you have answered and nodded that you are receiving interpretation in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, I did not understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I take it that what I am saying in English is being translated to you in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are here to give evidence and I need hardly remind you about that, and before I explain to you the procedure, I would kindly ask you to enter a solemn declaration, which is equivalent to an oath, that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth. This is required by our rules of evidence and procedure and the text of the solemn declaration has been prepared for you. It's contained in a piece of paper that has just been handed to you. Please read that solemn declaration aloud and that will be your undertaking with this Tribunal that you will be telling us the whole truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. You may sit down. And very briefly I'm going to explain to you what's going to happen. You will first be asked a series of questions by Ms. Korner, who is the chief officer, lead counsel, for the Prosecution here, and whom you have met already. She will be followed by Mr. Cunningham, who is defending Mr. Radoslav Brdjanin who is the accused in this trial. Mr. Cunningham is the gentleman to your left. You do not have any freedom, any right, to make distinctions between questions coming from the Prosecution and questions coming from the Defence. The Defence has got equal rights, as the Prosecution, to cross-examine you, to ask you questions, and therefore, you have an obligation which arises also from the solemn declaration that you have just entered, to answer each question that is put to you, irrespective of where it's coming from, as fully and as truthfully as possible. If you don't, you will incur the wrath of myself and of this Tribunal. Should you not understand a question or should you like a question to be repeated to you, you address me and I'll make sure that the question is clarified to you. If you need to refer to any documents which you may have with you or which you may be shown, you are free to do so. However, documents which you have or you may brought with you which are original and which are not yet in the possession of the Tribunal or of the Prosecutor as originals, you may and you shall be asked to produce them so that they can be checked, seen and verified. Of course, if you want them back you will have them back but you cannot refuse to show the Defence in particular any documents that you will be making use of. All right? Am I being clear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Having said that, having said that, I leave you in the hands of -- in the able hands of Ms. Korner, who will put to you a series of questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, could you give your name, please, to the Court?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: My name is Ahmet Hidic and I come from Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And were you born on the 22nd of December, 1946?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And are you a Bosniak by nationality?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, I'm going to in a moment ask you a few general questions about Bosanski Petrovac but I want to now deal with how you came to give evidence here. I think you originally made a statement in 1999 to an investigator from this Tribunal; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Subsequently, you were seen again a year -- roughly a year later, in July of 2000, and you were asked to give further details of the matters contained in your statement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And finally, as far as statements to this Tribunal are concerned, did you make a further statement the day before yesterday in connection with the documents that you had brought with you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And which I think you've brought the originals with you today, is that also right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if necessary, if the Court or the Defence wish to see them, you're prepared to let them be seen; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As far as any other interview is concerned, shortly after you were expelled from Bosanski Petrovac and whilst you were in Travnik, were you interviewed on film by a member of one of the international organisations that was present in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you there give an account of the events in Bosanski Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did that interview or at least part of it appear on a programme on Sarajevo TV called Witness to Genocide?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I think that that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I know that Your Honour has got the notes that I made during my interview with the witness yesterday. We do have the video here. We don't intend to use it because it's effectively the same as the evidence. I think you've got a transcript in any event but if the Defence wish to play it, it is available.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hidic I want then to turn please to the question of the documents just to deal with that, as a discrete topic. Did you return to Bosanski Petrovac on the 20th of September, 1995?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was that approximately a week after it had been retaken by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I think that that's right, between the 14th and the 20th, which is some six days.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When you returned to Bosanski Petrovac, in what sort of state was the town? And I'm talking about the town as opposed to the municipality.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Well, it was surprising for me, having been absent from Bosanski Petrovac for three years, to see that there were many troops, very few civilians. There were very few civilians there. And I got to meet some of my acquaintances but everything was vacant, wrecked, deserted. I hope this is enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As far as the municipal building was concerned, where the records are kept, was that occupied or what was that -- what was the state of that building?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: The building was vacant as well. And in a way, if I can say so, it was full of people. The people who were setting up a certain rhythm of life there. I entered the building for the first time not on the 20th but a day or two after that. Upon the invitation of the people who sent me to Travnik to central Bosnia to organise the return of the refugees back into Bosanski Petrovac. So they had already been some people there discharging certain administrative duties.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was happening to the records that had been kept within the assembly building or the -- I'm sorry, the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: The archive was strewn about, not only in the offices but all over, including the basement. The major part of the archive was simply strewn about everywhere and I saw a lot of records in the basement. The archive was available, was available to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, did you start to collect documents which related to the period of 1991 and 1992? In particular 1992.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Not immediately, since I had one month to organise the return of people. So sometime towards the end of the year and early 1996 I started collecting certain documents. People knew that I was doing that so they were bringing documents to me so that the documents who had some significance could be preserved.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And the people who were providing you with the documents, because you were interested in preservation of these records, who were they?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Mostly residents, clerks. In one word: Employees of the municipality from the reception clerk to, let's say, an officer of the municipality or at the time president of the War Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And those documents that you were provided with, did you keep them?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I kept what I received.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In some cases, did you make a note of the contents of the documents in a notebook?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what -- what impelled you, what was the criteria that made you record the contents of some documents in your notebook?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: It mostly had to do with documents from 1992, so let's say from May of 1992 until September, which is the period of time during which we Bosniaks stayed in Bosanski Petrovac. The documents mostly pertained to the meetings of the Crisis Staff, and they remained there in the municipal building after the withdrawal of Serbs from Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And did you then provide some of the documents, including your notebook, to the investigator, Mr. Grady, who you saw in July of 2000?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you bring with you to this Court other documents effectively those that you had made a note of in your notebook?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: These documents, the documents that are mentioned in the notebook are the ones that are photocopied except for a few documents which were new and which I have turned over to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, can I just ask, the documents that you were given by these people who were providing them to you, were they photocopies of the documents that were in the building or were they actual carbon copies of the documents?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: These are all originals and they come from the Office of the President of the executive board of Bosanski Petrovac municipality at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Have you ever had any connection with the Bosnian state organisation called AID?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ever make a statement to anybody from AID? Or speak to anybody?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ever provide to AID copies or originals of documents that you had received?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, can I ask you a little bit about Bosanski Petrovac? First of all, could you look at a map of the whole area known as the autonomous region of Krajina? It's P446.1. And we'll have it up on the ELMO. Now, Mr. Hidic, we can see, I think, at least if we are lucky, we can see, Bosanski Petrovac is towards the left of the map. Is it bordered by Kljuc, Sanski Most, Bosanska Krupa and Bihac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it's not shown on the map but did you also have a border with Croatia?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: No. We did not have a border with Croatia. We did not. Our borders went from Kulen Vakuf, so the borders of Bihac municipality, towards Bosanska Krupa, over the Grmec mountains towards Sanski Most, to the east towards Kljuc and to the south towards Drvar municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You're absolutely right. So although it's not marked it would be Drvar municipality, all right. Yes. All right. Thank you. Now we've established where it was in relation to the other municipalities. Thank you. That's all for that map. Now, could you look at, please, a census, a record of the census that was taken in 1971, 1981 and 1991, which is Exhibit P60? If you turn in that, please, to the second page, you will see it starts with Banja Luka and then -- no, if you go next page, turn it, I'm sorry, to the page that begins Banja Luka. Thank you. If we move down the list, we can see Bosanski Petrovac and for 1991, I think the total population was 15.621. The Croats were a tiny proportion, 48, 0.3. The Muslims, 3.288, 21 per cent. And then the Serbs were 11.694, forming 74.9 per cent. And I think as far as you're concerned that's obviously -- it's an accurate figure?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: The figure is accurate. However, I disagree with the first total number, 15.661 [as interpreted], because the records show there is a document that demonstrates that 15.552 residents lived in Bosanski Petrovac municipality according to the census of 1991. The percentages of the ethnic composition are approximately accurate.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The interpreter -- I had the interpretation say 15.661. And in actual fact at least in the document that I have, that we have, it says 15.621, just for the record, because it doesn't really make any difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's why I didn't bother to correct it. I heard that as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, yes, you needn't trouble with that document. But I'd like just to deal with figures in one go. Can you now look, please, at Exhibit P5 -- 56? Now, sir, I know you hadn't seen this document before you came to this Court. It's a document that was prepared apparently by Republika Srpska in May of 1993. It's stated to be a list of citizens who have moved out and into the area covered by the sector.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, just to be fair with the Defence, could anyone enlighten me as to whether this document was objected to by Mr. Ackerman? It was one of the documents objected to by Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think so but we will have to go back to the Banja Luka list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, perhaps Ms. Gustin can check that if she can.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We can certainly let Your Honour know after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. Just to know what the position is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I rather feel it comes from one of the seizures in 1998 in Banja Luka, and I don't think there was much objection to those.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we turn, please, in that document, and it's not suggested by any means, Your Honour, this is an accurate census -- to -- in the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Third page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Third page, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes it's the third page in B/C/S as well. Can you see item number 10 is Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In May of 1993, according to however this was compiled, 3.200 Muslims had moved out, no Croats, and 100 Serbs, and 4.000 Serbs had moved in. Now, you had left by then but would you agree that 3.200 Muslims had moved out?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I think that a larger number of Muslims left Bosanski Petrovac, not 3200. I believe that between 50 and 70 Muslims remained, because they were either members of the Serbian army and they had their families there, or they were quite infirm and were unable to leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you think by May of 1993, that instead of 3.200 having moved out, something in the -- well, in fact, there were 3.288 originally apparently in Petrovac in 1991 so that would be about right, wouldn't it? If you say there were about 50 people left?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So in other words, by May of 1993, barely a Muslim was left. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours Ms. Gustin has managed to look up her records and it was -- this document was admitted on the 18th of February, and indeed Mr. Ackerman used it during his cross-examination of BT21. So I think it was accepted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, you can put that away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Finally, ask I ask you to look at one more map before we deal with the substantive part of your evidence and that is a map of Bosanski Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Which will be a new exhibit, Your Honour. P1804.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No objections I take it from the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think Defence have got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: We don't have any objection to that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Cunningham. It's being so admitted as Exhibit P1804. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you had an opportunity to look at this map yesterday?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is clear, as we've seen from the census, that Petrovac was a large majority Serb municipality. Two villages have been marked, that is Bjelaj and Rasinovac as Muslim villages. Can you just tell us whether that's totally accurate in the sense whether there was a Muslim majority in those villages?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: It is absolutely not correct. Bjelaj and Rasinovac were villages inhabited by Muslims, but the population of these two villages is mixed, and those two villages are predominantly Serb villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But in -- I think -- that's intended to indicate in any of the other villages that are shown there, were there Muslims living or were they all Serb? For example, Kolunic or Medeno Polje?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I can say that all the other villages are currently Serbian villages, ethnically cleansed. However, previously, in these villages, there were also some Bosniaks and Croats, like in the town of Bosanski Petrovac itself, that is in the centre of the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. That's what I was going to ask you. For the town itself, which we can see marked, Petrovac, what was the mix of population there?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Also mixed according to the last census, there is a balance in the population, but some 20 or 30 years ago, it was predominantly Muslim or Bosniak urban area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And as we are going to hear, were there certain areas within Petrovac that were entirely inhabited by Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Obviously, the old streets or Mahalas as we call them were typically Bosniak or Muslim areas of residence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Looking at this map, where would you say, in 1991, 1992, was the biggest concentration of Muslim inhabitants? In which town or village or city or whatever? Looking at this map. Was there any where where there was a big concentration of Muslims? Or proportionately, I mean? There were 3.200, 3.300 Muslims living in the municipality of Bosanski Petrovac in 1991, according to the census that we -- you were referring to before. Where were they living? Was there any where in the municipality where there was a big concentration of Muslims? Or were they were just spread out everywhere but always in a minority in 1991?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1991, Bosniaks mostly resided in the so-called Mahalas or old streets, and if necessary, I can give you their names, in order to provide you with a clearer picture. So Biscani was a settlement inhabited by Bosniaks, up to the erection of the Skender Kulenovic residential area which was a new residential area that accepted a number of residents who were not Bosniaks. What I'm saying is that the lowest number of flats there were inhabited by Bosniaks. I'm -- so Didovici, Gaj, Ploca, Pekinska, were the names of the streets. All those were the streets with the highest concentration of Muslims. Obviously, the nucleus of the town was an urban area. That received the new settlers and they were predominantly Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think the point was this: Of the Muslims who lived in the municipality, did most of them inhabit the town of Bosanski Petrovac and the two villages that we can see marked in green on that map?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: That is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You can put that map away now or the usher can take it away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I've just got one more question and that deals with Petrovac as it is today. I think that the Serbs remained in Bosanski Petrovac until the army of the Bosnian Serbs pulled out in 1995; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: No. The Serbs left together with the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, that's what I meant. My fault. Then you told us that you were -- you became one of the people who was organising the return of the Bosniaks. Did the Serbs also start to return to Petrovac after the 1997 elections?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I think that your estimate of the present population is it consists of about 7 and a half thousand people, of which 50 per cent roughly are Serbs?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, can I turn to the events of 1991 and 1992? Was your job in 1991 and 1992 as a machine locksmith but also as the manager of a warehouse for a company in Bosanski Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in 1991 and 1992, were you a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: However, I think it's right you're today the President of the SDA in Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. These are the duties that I discharge and I was elected in 1999.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When did you actually become a member of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: During the war, in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to ask you about the relationships between the communities, the different ethnic communities in Petrovac before 1991. What were relations like really between the Bosniaks, as they are now called, and the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I believe that they were absolutely good, and there was a high degree of tolerance between Serbs and Bosniaks, and according to a popular story, we believe that the fraternity and unity was the strongest in Bosanski Petrovac. That is what politicians used to say when they were talking about the situation in Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What -- as a community, did most people know other people, if not to talk to, by sight? And particularly, I should say, the local politicians?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. People knew each other. They were very close relations. People were acquaintances. They were friends. Bosanski Petrovac is a small town and people knew each other regardless of where they resided, whether they resided in the urban part of the area or whether they resided in the rural part of the area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, can I turn to the municipal assembly? Did that have 50 seats?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, according to the elections that were held in 1991, there were 50 seats.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 1990, I think?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I apologise, it was in 1990.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I'm just going to put the results effectively you told us about. The SDS I think won 33 seats, the SDA 8 seats, the SDP 6 seats and the Reformist Party, 3 seats?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As far as the positions, the key positions, in the municipality were, was the President of the municipal assembly Rajko Novakovic of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The deputy president, Mustafa Ferizovic from the SDA?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: President of the executive board, a Mr. Latinovic, SDS?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the head of the police, a Dragan Gacesa?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the commander of the police was Mr. Kecman?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the head of the TO was an Obrad Vrzina?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Being members of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I want to move, please, to really how events progressed from 1990, in terms of the atmosphere. During the election period in 1990, were there rallies held in Bosanski Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Like elsewhere in Bosnia and Herzegovina, there were rallies in Bosanski Petrovac as well. That was all built up to the elections.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And was there any change, as it were, in the feeling between the ethnicities? Was there, as it were, more nationalistic feeling coming into the events?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: There was a turn in the relationship between the people, both in their private relations as well as at all the other levels of communication. I believe that the decisive factor in all that was the meeting of the SDS in front of the church in Bosanski -- that was the foundation of that party and that constituted a big turn in the relationships in Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, had there been or was there organised an exhumation during this period?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: The exhumations took place earlier. Some year before that. In 1990. And it took place in Risovacka Jama, some 20 kilometres away from the centre of Bosanski Petrovac municipality, in the local community of Krnjeusa somewhere between Krnjeusa local commune and Bosanska Krupa local commune.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the exhumation just briefly, because you say it was earlier, was of what?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: The remains of the Serbs who perished during the Second World War, at least this is what was said around the town these days, of the remains of those who died during the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was that exhumation used in any way to, as it were, incite nationalistic feeling?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a rally organised during the burial in Krnjeusa and that meeting was attended by all the leaders of the Serbian people, politicians and religious leaders so yes, I would say that this rally was used for political and nationalistic purposes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you say that it was attended by political and religious leaders. Can you remember any of the political leaders who attended?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I believe that Biljana Plavsic was there. I must say that Bosniaks, that is Muslims, could not attend such a rally. It never occurred to us to attend it, in any case. However, the Serbs who were there told us that Biljana Plavsic was there, that Raskovic came from Croatia, from the autonomous region of Krajina and there were some other politicians. I don't know who they were because I wasn't there and I didn't see them personally. As for the clerics, there was Pavle and also the Hrizostem of the Bihac and Petrovac area. And there were also politicians from the Bosanski Petrovac area obviously.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, you've told us there was also a rally outside the church during the run-up to the elections. Once the war started in Croatia, how did that affect the relationships between the ethnicities and what was happening in Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: The war in Croatia did have a huge bearing on the life in Bosanski Petrovac municipality. A lot of volunteers from Bosanski Petrovac went to Croatia and on their return, they expressed extreme radical tendencies and their behaviour changed and it never again was what it used to be before they went to Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before the war in Croatia began, had there been any military installations in Bosanski Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were any regular troops of the JNA stationed there?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Once it started, what was the situation in respect of military activity in Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I believe that at the beginning of the war, when a number of troops came from Croatia, Bosanski Petrovac, during those days, from the direction of Bihac and Knin, there were endless columns of motorised units of the JNA. Since I worked in Bosnaplast and this is on the road that leads via Drvar to Knin, I could see that these columns had a flag with a five-pointed star when they were leaving and on their return they did not have that flag. They had Milosevic's picture instead. These columns were on the move for maybe a month or even two months during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were any troops actually stationed in Petrovac itself?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Obviously, a lot of the troops of the former JNA were in Bosanski Petrovac. They were deployed in various places, mostly in those places where they could work or they could organise some details so they occupied factories, they occupied even schools or some recreational objects, and things like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were there any rallies held in respect of the JNA in Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. There was a rally. I believe that was when the last generation of recruits was being sent off to the JNA. A lot of the citizens of Bosanski Petrovac, both Serbs and Bosniaks, attended that rally and there were also representatives of the command and of the Bihac garrison who attended this festivity of sending of the last generation of recruits to the JNA and this rally served to express the support for the JNA by the Serbs and -- the words of support were used for the JNA during that rally.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'd like you to have a look, please, as Exhibit P1816. Now, this is a news item that was apparently on Bosanski Petrovac Radio, and it deals with a public forum, the JNA and mobilisation around the 2nd of November, 1991, and it talks about the people who attended, Colonels Vukovic, Vukelic, Skundric, Osman Selak and so on and so forth. And it describes -- it's really an open forum with questions in respect of mobilisation. Now, do you know, was this around the time of the rally that you just spoken to or is this the rally you were describing?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I believe that this was before the rally, and what I have just stated about the rally confirms the presence of these people on behalf of Bosanski Petrovac municipality, that is people who were in charge of that rally on behalf of Bosanski Petrovac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just ask this? Colonel Osman Selak, did you know anything about him? Had you ever heard about him before this or at all?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: No. I personally didn't know him. I didn't hear of him, but I believe that he came from the Bihac garrison.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Thank you. You can put that document away.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour I note the time. That may be an appropriate time for a break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we will have a 25-minute break -- 30-minute break. We will resume again at 11.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before we move on, Mr. Cunningham has requested that he be allowed to examine the original documents, plus his notebook, which Mr. Hidic has brought, over the luncheon adjournment so that Mr. Hidic understands, Defence counsel undertake to return them without doing anything to them but if Your Honour will --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, is that okay with you? Do you understand what Ms. Korner has --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So that's agreed. You will go through them, Mr. Cunningham, and then return them.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: At the lunch hour, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We've dealt with the increase of the military activity in Petrovac after the war in Croatia. Can we just for a moment consider the police in Petrovac? What was the ethnic makeup of the police force in Petrovac, roughly?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I am absolutely sure that 99 per cent of them were Serbs, so that was the ethnic composition.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, as far as the posts were concerned, the political posts, we've discussed the people who -- the head and command of the police. Was there ever a time when a Bosniak became the commander or a SDA member, I should say, of the police, which was the second rank, second position, in the police station?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I know that following the elections, there were negotiations held between political parties concerning the allocation of key offices, and that the SDA insisting on having its member as chief of police. However, that never materialised.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want to jump ahead, please, but on this topic to a document P1824, because it's dated the 11th of March, 1992. Now, this is the minutes apparently of the Crisis Staff on the 11th of March, 1992, and I'll deal as a separate topic with the Crisis Staff but on the agenda we see analysis and assessment of events of 10th of March, 1992, Mr. Novakovic talking about the administration of the Bihac security centre carried out personnel changes at the public security station in Bosanski Petrovac, against the will of the Bosanski Petrovac authority and Fuad Ferizovic was appointed commander of the public security station and other personnel changes. This caused public indignation, and I'll leave out the next sentence. In addition to the above-mentioned candidates, the SDS nominated Dragan Gacesa commander of the Bihac public security station, disgruntled at the changes the Bosanski Petrovac public security station set up several road blocks. Now, the first thing is the appointment apparently of Mr. Ferizovic was made by Bihac security centre. Did the police station in Petrovac come under the Bihac area?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was within the composition of the security centre in Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if you don't know the answer to this, do say so straight away, Mr. Hidic but what was the ethnic makeup in Bihac? Was it a Serb-controlled municipality or Bosniak, or was there a division?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I can say that there were 15.000 Serbs living in Bihac, and the composition was quite balanced when it came to the security services centre in Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, were you aware that a Mr. Fuad Ferizovic had been appointed commander of the Petrovac SJB?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I knew that he was nominated by the SDA. I knew that he was a lawyer with a proper degree and that prior to that, he was acting secretary of the health centre in Petrovac. As such, he was nominated to the post of the commander of the police station in Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did he ever take it up? Did he ever take that position up?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it says here that apparently road blocks were set up by members of the SJB in Petrovac. Do you remember that happening?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. However, that was probably done because of the very name of the person who was supposed to be head of the police administration. I think that this is what motivated it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. In the upshot, and we can see it through the documents, did Mr. Gacesa, as you told us, become the head of the police in Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. You can put that document aside now. Now, can we move to the topic of the, as it were, political alignment of Bosanski Petrovac? Did you become aware of the establishment of an organisation called the association of the Bosnian Krajina municipalities?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I knew about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I want you to look, please, now, at a document which is marked P5, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's in the Petrovac bundle behind divider 4, although it's an earlier exhibit. And at the same time, have P1813, because the two documents are linked.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a decision, the first document, P5, dated the 26th of April, 1991, of the Petrovac municipal assembly, which decided on the 10th of April, 1991, to separate the municipality from the Bihac intermunicipal regional association. And if you look at the second document, of the same date, also a decision of the municipal assembly, the decision there to join the community of the municipalities of Bosanska Krajina. I don't think we need go through that. Now, were you aware of this decision at the time?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. The very joining of Bosanski Petrovac municipality to the SAO of Krajina was publicly announced. Therefore, Bosanski Petrovac was the second municipality in Banja Luka region which after Bosansko Grahovo publicly announced it was joining it, so before Banja Luka joined. I am aware of that because that was announced on television as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, historically, was Petrovac part of the Bihac region or the Banja Luka region?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Petrovac, as far as I know, always gravitated and was in the composition of Bihac area, regardless of what type of administration was in place at the time, during the Austro-Hungarian empire, during the former Yugoslavia, and also just before the outbreak of the war, it was in Bihac area and there was a municipality association of three municipalities but that was all under the Bihac area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was the SDA and were the Bosniaks in Petrovac in favour of this?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I know that they walked out of the assembly session when voting on this decision on joining Bosnian Krajina was going on. I know that the SDP assemblymen voted against this decision. However, the SDS had a majority so the decision was adopted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'd like you to have a look, this is the last document on this topic, at Exhibit P1810. This appears to be the text of a radio broadcast and it appears to be an interview with Rajko Novakovic, the president of the assembly. It deals with the decision to leave and, as you stated, that the SDA did not vote in favour. And then Mr. Novakovic spoke about the reasons for joining the Krajina municipalities. He gives his reasons there, effectively because about the lack of benefit that you'd received, that the municipality had received from Bihac. Now, two questions. First, do you remember hearing him make that speech or broadcast?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: No. I personally did not. I believe that this was a news item prepared for the local radio station, because I can see there a signature of a journalist who was a journalist of Radio Petrovac at the time, Pero Dosen, I know him as a journalist and this was most probably announced on Radio Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we deal with that? It says -- it's got "P. Do" as a typed signature and we will see the related documents. That's a Mr. Pero Dosen, you believe?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you knew him personally, did you as a journalist for the radio?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And maybe obvious but what nationality was he?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: A Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The reasons that are given, though, were those reasons with which you as a citizen of Petrovac would agree?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Let me tell you, these are political reasons that prompted Novakovic into giving this statement. However, this here is not true. It is partially true but not entirely, because there were other municipalities in the region that lived under very modest circumstances. Their infrastructure was not regulated, as was the case in Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you look, please, then, at the next document, P1811, on the topic of Radio Petrovac? Addressed to Serbs and all upstanding people of Krajina. Let us stem the tide of fascism. Our houses, towns and villages are being torched and destroyed. We are fighting against Ustasha and Islamic fascists, scandalous lies, international conspiracy and so on and so forth. And finally, people of Petrovac, do not be taken in by any disinformation. You can get the real information by Radio Petrovac between 10.00 and 1300 hours every day except Monday because the station is provided with a permanent electrical supply. Now, there is no date on this. Perhaps you can help us. Did you hear first of all this particular broadcast?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I think that this was after the war had broken out. Radio Bosanski Petrovac commenced every working day with this type of proclamation.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So you're talking now about after April of 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So every day they would start with this kind of broadcast?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I have to point out that we Bosniaks were not able to follow the local broadcast, both radio and television, because we had power outages at the time when these types of programmes were broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before the war began, before April, 1992, was Petrovac broadcasting this type of -- trying to find a neutral word for it -- information?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: No. Not at all like this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And as far as the radio station was concerned, before April, 1992, who were the people running the station? What ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: All of the employees were Serbs. I don't know exactly how many employees they had, but there was just one employee who was a Bosniak, a lady announcer of Radio Bosanski Petrovac. Her name was Jasna Balic. Immediately, in the beginning, she was forced to read out an announcement that she did not agree with. She was forced to read it out. And following that, she was banned from entering Radio Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How did you come to know this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Jasna Balic was expelled together with me and other Bosniaks into central Bosnia, into Zenica. Before she departed to the United States, I used to have frequent contacts with her. We knew each other very well. This is what she claimed to me. She was forced by Milan Latinovic a retired journalist to read out an announcement following which she was fired.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think you're aware, Mr. Hidic, that if you can indicate when you give us a piece of information how you know it, that will assist the Court.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, on the subject -- thank you. The document can go back now. On the subject of telecommunications, then, please, where did Bosanski Petrovac receive its television programmes from in 1991?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Throughout 1991, Bosanski Petrovac had both radio and television broadcasts from the TV transmitter in Ostrelj which is an elevation of 1330 metres, so we received through that tower television programme from Sarajevo, and other studios that were -- formed part of that broadcast. And the same applied to radio programme. It also came from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did that change?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Absolutely. It did change. As early as 1991, Pljesevica which is above Bihac, and which was dominant elevation, supplying television signals from Croatia. Ostrelj was damaged or rather destroyed -- the TV tower there was destroyed. There were various rumours going around but the truth is that somebody did it on purpose in order to disrupt the broadcast of the radio television from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: After it had been destroyed, this tower, from where did you receive programmes?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: All broadcasts that we could follow, radio and television broadcasts, mostly came from Banja Luka area, from Banja Luka television, Belgrade, Novi Sad, Pristina, and Titograd television stations. So only these programmes were available to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did the programmes that you were receiving from Banja Luka, Novi Sad and the like, have any effect upon the relationships between the nationalities in Krupa -- in Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Naturally, absolutely. That had a huge impact. All of the information that we received represented only one side of the reality. We could receive no other information.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We saw this broadcast that Petrovac put out after the war started. Were the type of programmes that you were receiving before the war, before April, 1992, did they contain any of this type of material that we can see in that one?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I can tell you that all of the previous programmes, television programmes, were -- that were aired from Sarajevo studio were of a quite different nature. There was a programme of daily news coming from YUTEL television station that covered this area and it was followed both by Serbs and Bosniaks in this area and I heard very many positive comments regarding this programme.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll leave the topic. Now I want to deal with two events, then, at the end of 1991. Do you remember the Serbs holding their plebiscite?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think that it went on for two days.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I'd like you to have a look, please, at P1817. This appears to be a news report from something called Vijesti. Do you know what that is?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I believe that this is a local news, and this confirms what I have just said a little while ago. This was signed by Jasna Balic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And it talks about a meeting between the SDS and SDA in respect of this plebiscite. States that the position of the opposition parties is that national plebiscites do not solve problems and the opposition asks the main parties in Bosanski Petrovac, the SDS and the SDA, to preserve peace and unity. The opposition parties cannot and will not prevent their members from taking part in the plebiscite, and then they are concerned by the existence of ballot papers in different colours which leads in advance to division. Do you know what that's a reference to? And if you don't, say so straight away.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I can say that the political parties had frequent contacts. Personally I am not familiar with this and I cannot provide you with any comment on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. But then the bottom, can we just move, then, to the next part? The position of the SDA is that a plebiscite of the Serbian people and all others who are for Yugoslavia is unconstitutional and illegal. The SDA membership is also in favour of remaining in Yugoslavia but away agreed by all of us together and not in the way offered by a unilateral plebiscite in favour of a referendum of all nations and nationalities and so on. And then finally, the most important thing in all of this is that after reconciling positions concerning the plebiscite following the joint meeting, people went for a coffee together in the way that we in Bosanski Petrovac have become accustomed to doing. Would you agree with that last sentence, that that was the relationship between the Serbian and the Bosniaks in -- even in November, 1991, in Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. That was the relationship between the political representatives. They had daily contacts and it is possible that they did go and have a cup of coffee together and that's what the conclusion was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Taking it broader than just the political parties, would that be a summary of the relationship between all peoples, Serb and Bosniak, in Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I object. I'm going to object to the leading question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner, please do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's the attitude between the SDS and the SDA. How was that reflected in ordinary life between SDS members or Serbs, and Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: It is very hard for me to give you an answer to this question, given the time that has elapsed but I would say that the relationships in 1991 were still good. At least as far as the political parties are concerned. And even amongst the people, the general public, the climate was positive, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Now can we look at December, 1991? Could you be shown, please, P1818? I'm sorry, it's the wrong one. I beg your pardon, it's not the one I want. I'm so sorry. It's P1819. Now this is apparently minutes of a meeting of the SDS party Secretariat. We can see who the meeting was attended by. I just want to know if you know who these people are. Dragan Miljanovic?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know Dragan Miljanovic. He was not only a member of the Crisis Staff but he was a deputy as well, and a member of the SDS inner circle. He was one of the founders of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In Petrovac or nationally?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: In Bosanski Petrovac. I am talking about Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Nenad Dragisic?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know him personally as well. He has a bachelor's degree in economics.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Jovo Radojko?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
