utterances.text: I don't know this gentleman but I know that immediately before the conflict in Croatia, Jovo Radojko came to Bosanski Petrovac and that's where he originates from. He is a lawyer who had used to work in either Zagreb or somewhere in Croatia before the conflict in Croatia started. And if you will allow me, he was the secretary of the executive board of Bosanski Petrovac municipality after the elections.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Then very quickly, then, Mr. Knezevic?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Zdravko Knezevic, I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What position did he hold in Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I know he was one of the leaders of the SDS but I don't know what position he held. I don't even know whether he has any particular positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And finally Mr. Novakovic. Now we've seen him before but did you know Mr. Novakovic personally?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I did. I believe that he is somewhat younger than me but nevertheless I knew him very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just jump ahead. Is he still alive?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: No. He is not. Rajko Novakovic was killed in 1992. I believe that it was on the Grabez front line, when he was patrolling the lines and that was after the expulsion of Bosniaks from Bosanski Petrovac. This was maybe one or two months after that. I believe that this happened in November. The circumstances of his death were rather strange, if you will allow me. There were some controversial things involved in his death. There are stories on the one hand and there is an official version saying that he was killed by a sniper.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think he has finished Your Honour. I was going to stop him in any event.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Then that waives my objection Your Honour. My objection is moot now that the question is over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I want to move to some of the items that appear on this agenda or meeting. Item number 2, states that the instruction on the organisation and activity of organs of the Serbian people in Bosnia-Herzegovina in emergency circumstances needs to be typed in seven copies and every member of the Secretariat is to be given a copy. I want to ask you carefully about this. Did you ever in 1992 become aware of instructions being issued by the SDS to the main board SDS to local boards SDS?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: No. I was not aware of that in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. But we can leave out the, I think, items 3 and 4 and 5 but can we come to item 7, where it talks about, and this is December of 1991, Mr. Miljanovic, the deputy, raised the question of personnel changes in public enterprises. The vote was unanimous to replace the directors of the power supply company and the veterinary station and so on and so forth. Now, do you know in 1991, what the ethnicity was of these directors?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: The director of the power supply company was a Bosniak. That is a Muslim. The veterinary station as well, another Bosniak and the director of the postal services was another Bosniak. We are talking about managers, not directors.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It may be the translation -- what's the word in the -- in your copy? What does it say?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Directors.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Do you know, were these people replaced?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Before December of 1991, had there been any removal of managers or directors who were Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Before 1991, no. There were none.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This document is dated the 26th of December, 1991. After December, 1991, what happened to Bosniaks, first of all who were in positions of managers or directors?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: The few of them who were managers were removed, and replaced. Maybe there were one or two cases in which they had to stay on longer, and I'm talking about the head of finances in the municipality, who remained in his position up to mid-June, 1992. I was also active up to that time. I went to work, and I worked, and I believe that the two of us were the last Bosniaks who remained working in Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. One moment, Ms. Korner. Just to clear this up a little bit. You were referred to the directors of Elektrodistribucija and the veterinary station and I take it that you did confirm in your testimony that these two persons were removed from their positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You also mentioned because you were referred to that particular paragraph the director of the post telegraph and telegram service who you said was also a Bosniak. Was he also sacked?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, veterinary station, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Post telegraph and telegram service. He said that that person was also a Bosniak. Was he removed or retained in his position? Because the paragraph that was read out to you here says that while a decision, a unanimous decision was being taken to replace the directors of the power supply company and the veterinary station, support was being extended to the director of the post telegraph and telegram service and I understood you saying that this last director of the post telegraph and telegram service was a Bosniak. Was he a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes he was a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And was he retained while the others were sacked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that he was the last person to be removed. I don't know exactly when that happened. But yes, he was removed eventually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And why would you say, in this vote that was taken on this day, as related in this document, such a distinction was made between the -- this person and the other two Bosniaks that were sacked? Why would they decide to keep one and even extend assistance and support and sack the other two? Why would that be so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If this is important, I really don't know, but if this is important, I believe that this Bosniak was married to a Serb woman. I know his family name was Ferizovic, and that he was a professionally speaking indispensable. He was an expert in his field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Ms. Korner, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we deal with this? Here we see that these people have to be removed and you've told us that this went on until there were very few left. What reason was given to people, I'll come to your case in a moment, but from what you'd gathered, for removing them from their positions, Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: None of those who were removed were given any particular reasons. They were just sent away. They were told to go on holiday, and that was the only thing that we learned about these people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we come to your particular case? Although again we are jumping ahead slightly. You remained in your position until when?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I believe that I stayed on up to mid-June or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you think of any reason why you would have been kept on longer than other Bosniaks in their jobs?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I believe, and have believed all this time, that the reason was that I was the head of the warehouse which stored all the tools for the machinery in the fabric where I worked, and I was the only person who was in charge of that warehouse, and I believe that that was the only reason why they kept me on for such a long time. Eventually, I, as all the others, was told that I should stop coming, the key was taken away from me, and in my work book, the last day of my work, recorded in that work book was sometime towards the end of April, although I effectively worked up to mid-June or thereabouts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Roughly how many Bosniaks were left in their jobs by mid-June? As a proportion of working Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I've mentioned Mrs. Senada Mehdin who was a bachelor's degree in economics. She was the head of finances, and she was the last Bosniak to stay on. As soon as she completed her current -- her ongoing duties, she was said that she should not report for work any longer.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And when was that, roughly?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I believe that this was in the second half of June, between the 15th and the 20th of June. I can't give you the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The people who were dismissed, did any of them lose their apartments or houses as a result of losing their jobs?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: No, but those who left Bosanski Petrovac obviously they lost their property. It was in some other hands.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'll come on to that later. Now, then finally, please, on this document, in that same item number 7, it states that a meeting of the Crisis Staff was scheduled to be held in the Office of the President of the municipal assembly on the 30th of December, 1991. When did you become aware that this body calling itself the Crisis Staff was in existence?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: It was something that was known and we also knew that they met every day during the working hours, and in the evening. There were stories about that in the town and the information could be received from the representatives of the Serbs. Those were the people who could move around freely and so on and so forth. And they were the ones who spread this information, and we received that kind of information from those people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we try and put a time period? This is December, 1991. When was, roughly, when was the first time you heard from Serbs or from other people that there was this Crisis Staff? If you can remember.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I must say at this point that I really did not understand your question. I thought you referred to the Crisis Staff but there was no Crisis Staff in 1991. I believe that I have misunderstood your question. The Crisis Staff started existing sometime in April.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So that's what I'm trying to get at. You first heard about a Crisis Staff, the existence of a Crisis Staff in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the final question on this document is on the original, is there a signature? On the copy you've got, I'm sorry, the B/C/S copy?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And whose signature is that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Nenad Dragisic's signature.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think you told us that you knew him. Would you recognise his signature?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I would, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As far as you're concerned, is that his signature?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What about the stamp?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I am not familiar with this stamp. There were changes in Bosanski Petrovac municipality and the stamps were changed as well. So I'm not familiar with this particular stamp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you just tell us, though, what it says?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because it has not been translated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have some problems with my eye sight but I believe this is a stamp of the Serbian democratic party so this is a party stamp.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. I think does under the bottom of the shield, does that say Bosanski Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think I'll leave it to Judge Janu who can do this better than I can. All right. Yes, you can put that document away. Now, before we look at the activities of the Crisis Staff and what happened in Petrovac, did there come a time in Petrovac when freedom of movement became limited?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the question? I have not understood you clearly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: At some stage in Bosanski Petrovac, were there controls set up to prevent people from moving freely within Petrovac or leaving it?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. As early as 1999, there were some checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Sorry, the interpreter's correction, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There were some checkpoints where you had to show your ID. Otherwise you were not able to leave.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And did those checkpoints restrict everyone or just some people?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, at those checkpoints, only some vehicles and buses were checked, and as a rule, those were the buses on route between Bihac and Sarajevo. That is Bosniak municipalities. Later on, that control became more rigorous and if you will allow me, I would like to say that this checkups also involved military conscripts, who also had to produce some military IDs and Bosniaks had to state their reasons for leaving Bosanski Petrovac in a written form. They had to have a written explanation where they were going and why. And also that applied to military conscripts as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And briefly, please, on this topic, could you look at P1825? This Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 16181 to 16185. is a document dated the 1st of April, 1992, issued by the municipal assembly. But if you go to the end, is it signed by Mr. Novakovic and bears a stamp as well, as president of the people's defence council?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: The copy that I have is barely legible, as far as the signature is concerned and the same applies to the stamp imprint. It is quite unclear. So I couldn't tell from this. Perhaps you have a better copy.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm afraid we don't but what I just want to ask you about is, it states here he's not signing as president of the municipal assembly but president of the people's defence council. Was that a position that he held as well as being president of the municipal assembly?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Together with the Crisis Staff, which operated during April or rather during the beginning of the conflict, people's defence council operated in 1991, which means that it was established much prior to that. There were two Bosniaks in that council. One was the vice-president of the municipality and the other Bosniak was an official who worked in the people's defence, and at that time, for a brief period of time, he was appointed chief of the people's defence. And I think that this is why Rajko Novakovic signed this as president of the people's defence council.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the two Bosniaks on the council, how long did they last on the council?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Vice-president of the municipality remained there until the Crisis Staff was established.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, just two things on this document. Item number 7, the public security station in Bosanski Petrovac is instructed to ensure total control of passage and entry into the territory of Bosanski Petrovac of all persons. And then if we look at item -- now I've lost it -- oh, yes, I'm sorry, item number 8, the public security station in Bosanski Petrovac is obliged to prevent passage and if necessary apprehend all persons about whom there is reasonable doubt that they could threaten the security of Bosanski Petrovac citizens. Apart from the double negative, but in April of 1992, was this actually applied to everybody or was any particular section of persons picked upon?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: This pertained exclusively to non-Serbs. That is to say Bosniaks and Croats, who at the time moved through the territory. They were taken off buses and taken to police stations. As far as I know, it pertained to these persons. However, in the beginning, certain Serbs were also taken into custody.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But by this point, April of 1992, were certain Serbs still being taken into custody?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, I just want to deal by looking very quickly at the documents with the events of April, 1992. Can you look, please, although this is undated, but at the next exhibit, P1826? This appears to be a document addressed to the assembly of Republika Srpska and to the President, calling on them to protect the Serbian people in Croatia, on the territory of the Autonomous Region of Krajina, and states, furthermore we ask you to provide the necessary weapons to arm people so that the protected Serbian people, which was attacked during the Easter holiday of peace and love, can be defended. I want to ask you first of all about the allegation that there was an attack during the Easter holiday. Do you know what that was a reference to?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's a request, and as we can see, it's signed by or there is a signature, that says Mr. Novakovic, asking for weapons to arm people. Did you notice in Petrovac any increase in persons carrying weapons, Serbs carrying weapons?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I personally did not see it but every night I could hear the sounds of shooting, bursts of shots fired in Bosanski Petrovac, that took place in 1991 and especially at the beginning of 1992, prior to the outbreak of war. That was a daily occurrence. One could hear shots fired both during various celebrations, festivities, one could hear automatic fire opened regularly based on which I conclude there was a large number of weapons in Bosanski Petrovac before the outbreak of war.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. You can put that document away. Can you look, please, as Exhibit P1827 which really just confirms what you told us earlier. It's in fact two documents. This is document signed, both signed by Mr. Novakovic, apparently, again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's for Rajko Novakovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is it? So it is, Your Honour, thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At least the first one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think they are both za. Yes, they are, sorry. On his behalf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It shows that the assembly, on the 10th of April, relieved Mr. Ferizovic of the veterinary surgery of his duty. They appointed Suljo Kartal an employee, as the acting director. What nationality was he?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Suljo Kartal is also a Muslim, but this requires an explanation. Enver Ferizovic refused to be mobilised and to be sent to Kupres as director of veterinary station and this is why he was removed from office and Suljo Kartal immediately upon his appointment, was deployed within a unit that was sent to battlefield in Kupres.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. But he was in fact a Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Also a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then if we look at the next document, in that -- in that bundle, that's all right. That shows Mr. Ramic, Ahmet Ramic, the electrodistributor, shall be relieved and Mr. Milorad Bursac to be appointed as acting manager. Mr. Ramic, being a Bosniak, and Mr. Bursac being a Serb, we take it?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, can we look at, please, the events in later April and May? Did there come a time when there was an order to disarm?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, naturally. There was -- there was. There even was a proclamation on disarming and collecting weapons from Muslims exclusively. That applied both to sports weapons and all other kinds of weapons. Muslims were required to surrender them before a certain deadline.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can you remember now when that was roughly? I mean we've looked at documents from April. Was it in April or May or later?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I think it was in May that this activity took place in May.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how was the order given? In other words, by public announcement in newspapers, over the radio? How?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I think that in this case, there was an announcement over local radio and also personal calls were made to people who were recorded as owners of weapons with a licence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And who issued the order to disarm?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: This came from the police administration, from the police station.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, you say it was exclusively to the Muslim population, and it applied to sports weapons and all other kind of weapons. Did you yourself own any kind of a weapon?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Once time for the deadline of handing these weapons in had passed, what actually happened?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I think that the urban settlement of Bosanski Petrovac was blocked after that and the search was conducted in some houses, not all of the houses were searched, only certain houses, but definitely a large number of houses were searched by policemen, both active and reserve forces that had already been activated at that time. So the reserve forces had been activated earlier and they were involved in this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was there any demand that Serbs who were not serving in the army should surrender their licensed weapons or any weapons they had?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Not at all, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: As far as you were concerned, did the Bosniaks in Petrovac pose any threat to the Serbs who lived in Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Both now and then, when that was going on, I can say that Bosniaks represented no threat whatsoever to the Serb population in Bosanski Petrovac municipality, not only because they were an ethnic minority in that town but they were no threat whatsoever. They represented no danger to Serb people.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was there any kind of resistance to what the Serbs were doing to the Bosniaks? And by that, I mean violent resistance, shooting at Serbs, resisting searches or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any such thing and I believe, and I claim that not for a single moment was there any resistance or any activity of that sort against Serbian authorities, either the military authorities or the civilian authorities in that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: People were asked to -- I say asked -- ordered to surrender their weapons. Did any Bosniaks that you know, either refuse to hand in their weapons or attempted to obtain weapons?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I don't know of any such attempts, but I'm sure that there were such attempts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were there any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's get this clear, because your question, Ms. Korner, was referring to two separate or different actions. One either refused to hand in their weapons or attempted to obtain weapons. And he is saying that he doesn't know of any such attempts but he's sure that there were such attempts. Attempts at what? Are you aware or are you sure that there were Bosniaks that refused to hand in their weapons? Let's take them one by one. You said that you don't know of any cases but...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nobody refused that, there was not a single case registered of anybody refusing to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And with regard to attempts to obtaining -- to obtain weapons, you said you don't know of any cases but you're sure that there were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Of course. There were people who obtained weapons. They were able to buy weapons, and those weapons had already been registered or had previously been bought by Serb soldiers or other Serbs. So one could purchase weapons and such weapons would then fall on the investigation and it was confiscated later on by the police after the investigation had been carried out because all these weapons were registered. These weapons all arrived from the front lines through various channels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think if I read you well, Ms. Korner, that your question was not directed actually to any attempt to acquire weapons in a regular manner because we are referring at a time -- referring to a time when there was a call for the surrender of weapons. So Ms. Korner's question must be answered within the context of that particular event, and so I repeat the question: Were there any Bosniaks that you know of or that you believe that did not actually hand the weapons to the authorities when they were asked or called upon to do so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not aware of any such thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: During the same period, were there attempts by some Bosniaks to acquire weapons, to acquire weapons in a clandestine manner, not in a legal manner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There were such attempts. I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we now have it placed within the proper context. Yes, Ms. Korner, sorry to have butted in like this but I needed to clarify this in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was my fault because I asked a two-fact question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I now want to look, please, at how the Crisis Staff dealt with events in Petrovac after May or during May and after. Could you look, please, at P1829?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour what I propose to do is indicate when I go through the ones, the documents that he's actually provided for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Exactly. This is what I was going to ask you because these -- I don't know whether all of them are replicated but it seems that the majority of them are. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, none of the documents that he's provided we have received from other sources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: They are all completely no -- except that he brought with him a further copy of one which he had earlier given us but there is no replication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exhibit 1829 is minutes of the 15th session of the Crisis Staff of Petrovac and we see that -- who the members of that Crisis Staff were. They include a Lieutenant Colonel Sovilj. I think that's right. Did you know who he was?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I personally don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The agenda starts with definition of the procedure regarding the order by the Banja Luka regional Secretariat for National Defence, and I think Your Honour will find that relates to the disarmament order if we want to look back at the gazettes but I want to ask you about -- if you can move, please, it's page 4 in the translation. It's the decisions. It's decision number 2 which talks about shooting in public places. In the B/C/S, I don't know, it's -- I think it's on the third page. Thanks. Shooting in public places and all other shooting is strictly prohibited because such a misuse of ammunition endangers security and jeopardises the defence capacity of the Serbian people and so on. Did you notice -- you described how there was a lot of shooting going on at night. Did you notice there was a reduction after this order?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: It's a very difficult question but this only confirms the fact that what I have just said really did happen. There was a lot of shooting on the daily basis, and I don't think that this was reduced at any point in time. It continued and all sorts of intimidation continued especially in the urban area, in the town, and if you will allow me, especially before the soldiers were leaving for operations, for the front lines, this increased and the intensity of all of that would step up.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then item number 3, of the decision, or decision number 3, commission is being set up to draw a proposal for insignia that will be displayed publicly, ways of displaying Serbian flags so on and so forth and a possible change of name of the town and street names in Bosanski Petrovac. Was there a change, forget about the Serbian flags and all the rest of it, but was there a change of name for various street names and for Petrovac itself?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I did not notice these changes, so the decision -- there was a decision to change the name of Bosanski Petrovac. Everybody voted against it except for the members of the SDS. I think that in May, Bosanski Petrovac lost the Bosanski prefix and it remained simply known as Petrovac as was proposed by the SDS assemblymen in the assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Briefly in the last -- that's it for the document, thank you. In the last few minutes before we break, there is a reference there to the autonomous region, it's the Secretariat for National Defence, in later documents that you've provided, there are references to the Crisis Staff of the region. Did you become aware that there was a regional Crisis Staff in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you that because I didn't know it at the time. Later on, we learned that there had been such an organisation and that it was in operation but at the time I didn't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So when you say later on, is that when you returned and looked at the documents?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: No, no. Later on, I learned from people in town that there were such institutions in operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Later on, how --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was publicly discussed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Later on, when? You learned later on. How much later on? When? When did you learn about the existence of the regional Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During my stay in Bosanski Petrovac, until the day we left that town. So that means sometime between May and September, during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: While these dismissals and acts against Bosniaks were continuing, were you still -- were Serbs still talking to Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I think that there had been contacts, but that they were already under pressure. People were afraid of meeting personally, having contacts with somebody in public places, but there had been contacts until the last day between Serbs and Bosniaks, and by this I'm referring to ordinary citizens, but there was a certain dose of fear involved.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, because you say you heard about the regional Crisis Staff through Serbs talking - let me find the words - from other people in town who I think -- I'm not sure it's come up on the screen, but I think you said that there was -- it was from Serbs telling people?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: If it is of any assistance, I can tell you that I had a friend, a retired policeman, who had been reactivated. We had frequent contacts and while talking to him, I learned certain things and to be quite frank, I didn't need that information. I just happened to learn that from that man. I can give you his name. It is Milovan Atlagic. He was a retired policeman in Bosanski Petrovac. My neighbour and childhood friend.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we need to stop here, yes. So we'll have a lunch break now and we'll resume at 2.00. Thank you. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.30 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour before the witness comes in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think it appears his notebook wasn't in -- I'm sorry, I see Mr. Cunningham is on his feet but it appears his notebook wasn't in this envelope so we are not sure whether he did bring that. I don't know if Your Honours want to see. Those are the originals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will have a look at them. Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Shall I hand them to Your Honour's legal officer and then I'll explain to Mr. Hidic or Your Honours can explain that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please. Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, sorry interpreters. Mr. Cunningham do I take it that you want to address the Trial Chamber about the next week's schedule?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Yes, sir. The Court asked me to go into the prospect of us working a full day each day next week and I would respectfully ask the Court that we not do that subject to what I'm about to tell the Court. When Mr. Ackerman approached me about getting on this case it became clear to me and your subsequent pronouncements have made it even clearer that should Mr. Ackerman not be able to continue it's going to fall on to my shoulders to be able to step into the void and assume the role as lead counsel for the defendant. I have no problem whatsoever with that. That was made clear to me from the start but in order to do that job, I've had to go through and I am still I've barely cracked the surface of reading the transcripts. I believe we are in our 184th day of trial. I've read very, very few days of trial even though I'm trying to read at least two, three days of trial testimony at night. So that makes it difficult for me on an extended work schedule to, one, prepare for participate in the proceedings, two, prepared for the next day and three, get caught up. There is an additional problem that's occasioned by the fact that we are without our case manager. As we found out yesterday, it is very, very difficult or two days ago, found out it's very difficult to conduct a full day's proceedings get to the detention centre and have any meaningful conversations with the defendant. We are trying to do that as best we can during breaks. But quite candidly we are hampered by the fact that we do to the have the case manager, and I'm still figuring out the system. I have no doubt of my ability to participate in this process or get up to speed but I would respectfully ask the Court no to not sit late next week. Now, having said that the Office of the Prosecutor has approached me and as you know from their prior conversations, there is a witness who has had a number of work problems, work-related problems. I sympathise with those problems and I think we have reached what I hope the Court considers a happy medium and a compromise and that is we would work late Monday and Tuesday, full sessions, as if today, to accommodate this witness, as well as the witness that has the work problems so I hope the Tribunal finds that to be a happy medium and I'll say in advance that so as to avoid a recurrence of what happened with the past witness, last witness, who had to come in today for maybe 15, 20 minutes, if the Court's schedule permits, I can say I have no problem extending beyond the 4.30 hours to ensure that that witness makes it home.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. Cunningham.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand the problem and much though I would like to be able to invite Your Honours to sit while we've got the opportunity a full day, I know the problems with the Defence and I don't think it would be right to raise -- I would however like if I may, to -- and Mr. Cunningham has agreed, Monday and Tuesday because there is this witness and the second witness from Petrovac he's the one with the work problems. There is then Mr. Kaiser who has agreed he would be able to testify on Wednesday. We anticipate he will be through in one session, I mean one sitting of the court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So are we agreed that we will work extended hours only on Monday and Tuesday?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is that okay with you, Mr. Cunningham?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So be it. Madam Registrar, you will make the necessary adjustments to the Court schedule. All right? That's okay with you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TAYA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose we can bring in the witness and we can proceed, if there is nothing else that needs to be said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We all agree on that one, Your Honour. I would be happy if we get rid of this utterly useless equipment from here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's all crammed, everything is crammed in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm afraid the British have to take responsibility for this Court as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, so all you need to do is to effect the changes in the official court schedule because the public ought to have a right to know, to start with. All right? Otherwise we can proceed. Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will be proceeding. Ms. Korner will continue with her examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Mr. Hidic, just so you know the Judges have your documents at the moment and will be handed back to you at the end of the day I imagine?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So these Mr. Cunningham hasn't seen as yet?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, he has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He has. What I wanted to know is one thing. There seems to be some or quite a number of paragraphs and sometimes just sentences which have been underlined in blue by a pen or whatever. Did you underline those paragraphs and those sentences or was it someone else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was me and only me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher? I thank you. Give them back and we needed to clarify, did you get everything that you wanted, Mr. Cunningham, during the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: We did, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, we were talking about the regional Crisis Staff just before the break and I now want to ask you about Mr. Brdjanin. First an easiest question have you ever met Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you ever see him in Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: No, not personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In 1992, were you aware of Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. When was the first time that you heard of Mr. Brdjanin?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I believe that I heard his name on one of the TV shows. I don't know which one.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: It was sometime in 1992, during the period that we are talking about. I don't know whether it was at the beginning of that period in March or in April, I can't really tell you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You say you believe you heard his name on television. Did you ever hear him personally speak, either on television or on radio?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What position in 1992 did you understand Mr. Brdjanin to hold?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Personally, I didn't know anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. So you heard him on television --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He heard about him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, heard about him. Yes, you're quite right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Heard about him on television. In what context, can you remember?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I really can't tell you at this moment because at that very moment I didn't pay too much attention to that. It didn't concern me directly. In other words, I personally was not interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Did you know whether or not he had anything to do with the regional Crisis Staff that you told us you heard about?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I can't give you a positive answer. I was not absolutely sure. I'm not sure that I knew that at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Did you hear his name mentioned on television once or more than once?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: What I could follow and hear on television while I could, I believe that I heard his name, the name of Brdjanin, being mentioned one in a certain context.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you can't recall the context any longer?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I can't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Don't worry. How much interest did you take in politics in 1992?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I didn't take any interest in politics at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Let's -- can we then move on to deal with the events as they unfolded in Petrovac? Perhaps using the documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, the next document I'm going to ask to produce but I don't know if we need take the witness through it, is the Crisis Staff minutes dated the 21st of May, 1992, because that's a new document produced by Mr. Hidic, and Your Honour may I ask that that be marked Exhibit P -- I think Your Honours and the registry were given a bundle of these.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are talking of 21st of May, correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's the 21st of May with the number KS 10/92. Except --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This will be P?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: P -- I'm sorry. P1805. 1805. The only --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all, perhaps you ought to confirm, Mr. Hidic, that's one of the documents you were given, is it?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The writing that we can see on the -- there, this handwriting on the first page, was that written by you or by somebody else?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: It was written by me.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And it --

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Are you talking about the upper right corner where it says, "2/95" I can't say correctly recorded in the book. This is my handwriting, and this is what I wrote. And this book is the notebook, a photocopied notebook that was made available to this Trial Chamber earlier on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right. And we can see a reference to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the notebook itself, I think, or the photocopy, had better also be produced as an exhibit at this stage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That will be 1806.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, I'm not going to take you through this except for this: The Crisis Staff spent a whole meeting effectively talking about cows. And it is described as the distribution and accommodation of cattle brought from the areas of immediate war operations. This is a recurring theme throughout these minutes. Were cows of importance in Petrovac, as a matter of interest?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Zelenbaba thought so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't catch that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Zelenbaba thought so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, well, quite.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But it's perhaps unusual to see so much time spent on cows in a municipality. So perhaps you can just help us on that.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: In a nutshell, this was war booty. The cows were from Kupres and the vicinity where the aggression had taken place and all the cattle was collected as war booty and this has to do with me as well, because I was still working at the Bosnaplast. This was the logistical centre and this is where the cattle was initially accommodated and later on they just disappeared and I can see here that they were dwelling upon this issue for quite sometime.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. That can go back to the Registry. Could you now look at a set of minutes from the 24th of May, again a document that you provided. Actually, just -- oh, yes, there are three of them. This is the one with the number, sorry, quite right, KS 13/92, that's it. I just want you to identify this is one of your documents and your hand -- and your writing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This will be 1807?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can borrow mine.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You sure?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, one of the documents that was given to you, Mr. Hidic?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And again is it your writing in the top, right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Can we just look at the decision, please, at the end of that document? Where it says the executive board will ask from companies and organisations to provide plans of production and work during wartime. And then the companies and organisations which fail to meet this request completely shall be held responsible to the Crisis Staff and the executive board is hereby authorised to change the managers of such companies following a consultation of the Crisis Staff. Item 2, ethnic Muslims shall be engaged in the companies and organisations in accordance with the need, i.e., at the request of the companies and organisations which employ them. This brackets request must be based on the needs determined in the agreed plan of war production. Jovica Sepa voted against this decision. Do you know this person?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I know who Jovica Sepa is. He was an official. He was one of the top officials in the general administration, and the administration for the economy, and he was also given the mandate to be in charge of all the activities regarding the people's defence when the former person in charge, who was a Muslim, was dismissed. So he was in charge of all the activities regarding people's defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did your company go on to some kind of what's called a wartime schedule?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: My company was among the first that went to a wartime schedule, and it was proclaimed a logistical centre already in 1991, between the month of September and the month of November, when it was organised as a company which included a logistical centre and if I may add to that, my director was one of the -- one of those who were appointed in the chain of the military structure as one of the heads of the logistical centres. His name was Matincevic [phoen] and he was a technology engineer. He was -- who was in charge of production. He also had a rank, a reserve rank. He was a reserve non-commissioned officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop here for the time being. Could the witness be shown, please, Exhibit P1819 which he's seen already this morning? And the reason for doing so, Ms. Korner, is that when you went through the list of the members present at the first meeting of the party secretariat, the SDS, held on the 26th of December, 1991, between Jovo Radojko and Zdravko Nedznevic [phoen], you skipped the person who -- whose name was not exactly too clear. Jovica Sepa. Sir, could I ask you to look at the B/C/S version of that -- of those minutes? First paragraph, second line, you have Jovo Radojko. Could you read the next name? Would that be the Jovica Sepa that you have been referring to now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Jovica Sepa who was also a member of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So whoever read that as Jepa [phoen] was wrong. It should be Sepa according to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sepa is the correct pronunciation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we have a completed the team of persons attending that meeting now.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour that's very helpful. And in fact, if Your Honours look at P1831 I'm not going to trouble the witness with it but there you will see the list of the members of the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I have just one last question, please, Mr. Hidic on this document. And that is this: Were you aware of any request being made that you should stay on in your company? In other words did your manager or whoever tell you that they'd made a request?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. That's that document. Thank you very much. Can we move to the second document for the 24th of May, which is the one with the number 14/92? Which is Exhibit 1808, please. And again, I don't -- very briefly, it talks first about military arrangements and then we are back to cows and the decision is that all cows which were stolen from a farm in Medeno Polje, where is Medeno?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Medeno Polje, if I may say, is seven or eight kilometres from the centre of the town, and this was a place where a farm was, and it still is, and this is for raising cattle owned by the combine of Bosanski Petrovac. During the war it was used to accommodate these cows which were a war booty taken from the entire area of Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Then the last one, please, for that day?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This will be 1808.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I think I said, sorry, Your Honour, it's 1808, for the 24th of May, which is 16/92, which will become 1809, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Again, is that one of the documents that you were given, Mr. Hidic, and which has your writing on the top right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And if we look at the last page, it's got a signature on it but no stamp?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... you in regards to which copy such -- of the minutes this would be?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I think that following each session of the Crisis Staff, there were several copies made and it is most likely that certain copies were not stamped, that means they were signed but not stamped by clerks who normally did that. This isn't just an isolated example. There were many examples like this. There were more copies made than the number of Crisis Staff members attending the session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, you obviously didn't attend the sessions yourself. How do you know this is what was happening?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I suppose that that was the case, because there is a large number of documents, not signed and not stamped, that were found following the liberation of Bosanski Petrovac. They were found either in the archives that were in disarray or in -- within certain records in certain offices.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And did you -- you told us that you yourself went into the municipal building and saw these documents. Do you yourself notice unsigned copies and signed but not stamped, in the municipal building after the BiH Army had come in?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I saw such documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now I want you to look, please, just at one aspect of this meeting and how it impacted on the lives of Bosniaks in Bosanski Petrovac. Item number 3 of the decision. Premises within the building of the public security station Petrovac will be prepared for detaining perpetrators of criminal acts, perpetrators of flagrant criminal acts, criminal acts against safety and criminal acts that jeopardise the defensive ability of the Serb people will be detained in a prison until a trial. Prisoners in custody can be utilised for work of a public interest as well as on jobs related to defensive preparation, building of shelters, transport of military equipment, and other things. That's parts underlined. That's your underlining, is it?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think that I underlined that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Now, it's said here that the premises within the public security station can be used for detaining people. Were people -- did people after the 24th of May, Bosniaks, I'm sorry, not people, were they arrested?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is true that these premises were designated for this use in the basement of the police station in Bosanski Petrovac, and it is true that people were detained in those premises. Finally, those premises were not large enough to accommodate all of those who were brought into that building, and I'm referring here to Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. We are going to move on to what then happened because the police station was not large enough but the Bosniaks who were being arrested, from your knowledge -- first of all, did you know people who were arrested?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I did [Realtime transcript read in error "didn't"] know them. I also had occasion to talk to them following their release or following their departure from the camp in August.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I thought you said you did know them but it's been translated as you didn't?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters's note, I believe that I said I did know them.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know some of those people-- some of those persons personally.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were they told why they were being arrested?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: They were mostly arrested because they were suspected of being in possession of weapons. There were some other reasons as well, but most of them were arrested because they were suspected of owning or possessing a firearm. These were mostly people who had private businesses, catering establishments, shops and so on. They were mostly people who had a prominent standing in Bosanski Petrovac municipality, members of the Muslim community.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now then it goes on to say that prisoners in custody can be utilised for work of what's described as a public interest and then for defensive preparations. Were people made to carry out this kind of work, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: The people I had contacts with were not made to do that but some were used to unload humanitarian aid that was arriving at the time, flour, foodstuffs and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then if you just look at, please, item number 5, which is an order to the Petrovacka Brigade. What was the Petrovacka Brigade, if you know?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Petrovac Brigade is a formation that was established towards the end of 1991, early 1992. Initially, it was located in the sports hall within the secondary school centre. That was in fact a battalion that later on was used as a nucleus once the Petrovac Brigade was established.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, that's all you need that one for. Can we move, then, please, to the next document you supplied, which is the minutes of the 28th of May, which bear the number 17/92. And it's -- it's 1865, now, Your Honour, because we are now on the Petrovac binder. We used up some unused exhibits. Numbers, rather. Again, sir, does that bear your writing in the top right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's my writing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, in item number 1, there is Mr. Miljanovic informing the meeting of the results of the talks with the representatives of the SDA citizens forum. Can you tell us what this SDA citizens forum was?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: It wasn't the SDA citizens forum. It was the citizens forum of the citizens of Bosanski Petrovac. The SDA citizens forum is a political party so it's a different thing. People mentioned below Safet Hidic and Mustafa Ferizovic were representatives of the SDA whereas the citizens forum was an independent body established in cooperation with the representatives of Serb authorities and that body had contacts with Serb authorities in Bosanski Petrovac. It was aimed at criticising the SDA and facilitating the cooperation with the SDS. And people in it were exclusively people from the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And when you say that it was aimed at criticising the SDA, in what respect?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Let me clarify this. The citizens forum consisted of people who were either in mixed marriages or were former communists in power earlier, or with close ties to the former authorities in the former Yugoslavia, not just Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what sort of activities were they undertaking?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I think that their main activity dealt with the issues concerning preparations for the moving out of Muslims from Bosanski Petrovac. This is what they discussed in contacts with representatives of Serb authorities who had very little time for them, just like for other representatives. I also think that the citizens forum had an important role concerning the status of camp mates who were imprisoned in camp. They attempted to establish contacts with the international community and with authorities in Bosanski Petrovac in order to secure release of people who were imprisoned in camps. Some of their children or family members were in the citizens forum.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's just look briefly at what they were doing apparently in the discussion that was reported. The SDA representatives were said to be spreading alarming rumours by saying that Muslim citizens want to emigrate collectively but according to Dragan Ivanic, the citizens forum has an unanimous stand with respect to the Muslims being loyal citizens and supporting the authority. Mr. Ivanic being who?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Dragan Ivanic is the President of the municipal board or rather the executive board of the SDS in Bosanski Petrovac municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And then they accuse Mr. Hidic and Mr. Ferizovic of illegal arming. Safet Hidic, was he any relation to you?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: We are relatives but not close relatives. We do have the same family name.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Mr. Ferizovic apparently accused of illegal arming. Did you know both these gentlemen, Safet Hidic and Mustafa Ferizovic?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Naturally, I knew them.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you aware of them providing illegal arms to the Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I didn't know. However, I was an eyewitness when Mr. Safet Hidic personally surrendered to the police his rifle, explaining that he did have a rifle. The police came into his yard and he personally turned over his weapon to the police men who came there. We lived on the same street so that's how I know this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And was this at the time of the disarmament process that you spoke about?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely then.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And we are back to cows again and finally, please in the conclusion, it says, men under 60 must not leave the territory of the Petrovac municipality until the situation of the illegal arming of the Muslim people is carried out or investigated. At this stage of the game, at this stage of the proceedings, were people -- were Bosniaks or people who wanted to allowed to emigrate?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I think that following the expiration of the final ultimatum which was at the end of May, it was impossible to leave Bosanski Petrovac without Serb authorities knowing about this. It was impossible to leave without a pass or without having somebody guaranteeing for those who were leaving Bosanski Petrovac. It was impossible to leave without the knowledge of the representatives of Serb authorities. It was especially impossible to go into the direction of Bihac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. That's all I want to ask you about that document. Can you look, please, for a moment, but I don't think we have the one for this. Just a moment. I just want to check the numbers. Yes. You'll need to look, please, at the photocopy of your own notebook because I don't think we have got the document for this one entry, which is the document that was attached to the statement and is now P1808 -- 06, I'm sorry. Actually don't trouble. I think I'm anxious to get on so don't worry about that, no. Can we move, though to the next document we haven't looked at before, seen before, the 1st of June minutes which are numbered 22/92? And can you just identify those as another document that you have provided and again which contains your writing at the right-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honours could that be made P1866?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then could you now be handed the next document, also dated the 1st of June but KS 23/92?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, are you going to give this last document and the previous one separate number from Exhibit number from P1865 and 1866 because 1865 and 1866 I think the original or the source is different, no? Or are they --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: These are all new documents, Your Honour. These are all still from him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Still from him. So the one we saw last, is it going to be 1866 or 1865? Or 1811? Is there a reason why --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: There was a whole new binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there a reason why we have jumped from 1809 to --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, sorry, I don't know whether Your Honour obviously missed that I said what we did was use up unused exhibit numbers then we've got the binder and now we are going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That explains it. I did misunderstand everything actually.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this is 1866. The previous one remains 1865.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what I hope the witness, Your Honours, now have in front of you is 1st of June with the number 22/92.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And this will be 1867.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And this will be 1867, absolutely, thank you, Your Honour. And I don't actually think other than -- I think you've already said this is your handwriting in the right-hand side of the first page, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think other than that, there is anything that I want to draw your attention to. Then on the same day a lot of meetings again on one day, it's the 1st of June, 1992, with the number 23/92.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour I'm sorry, I think we've lost track slightly of the exhibit numbers now. Can we just do a confirmation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's all my fault, I think, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have mixed you up because I referred to the previous one as 1867 myself when it should have remained 1866 so this new one, KS 23/92 which becomes 1867.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I apologise for the mixup.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's all right. And again, Your Honour, I think -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can you just look, please, at item 2 on that document? The Crisis Staff has also discussed the situation in the territory of the Petrovac municipality regarding the emigration of some SDA representatives. The Crisis Staff has concluded that the best solution at the moment is the said representatives stay in Petrovac for the benefit of their people. Did you know any of the SDA representatives who wanted to emigrate?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I would like to take this opportunity to say that Mr. Safet Hidic, leader of the SDA, upon the consent of the municipal board of the SDS, on the 3rd of June, left the territory of Bosanski Petrovac. He was taken by the same man to a checkpoint in Lecin [phoen], and after that he crossed on foot over the bridge to the other side, to the settlement called Golubici from where he went to Bihac. So the President of the SDS directly assisted the President of the SDA in leaving the area and going to Bihac. There were other four people accompanying him.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What about other members of the SDA? Were any who wished to leave prevented from so doing?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I think that another prominent member of the SDA, Mustafa Ferizovic, as vice-president of the party and vice-president of the assembly, was also in Bihac at the time. I think that he left between the 20th and 30th of May. He went to Bihac area and his departure was also organised by some representatives of the authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. That's all I want to ask you on that. Could you have the next document, please, which is dated the 2nd of June, and is number 29/92? P1868. Thank you. I wonder if you could -- could you fine the original, please, sir, in your bundle, of that document? In your -- the ones you brought with you, sorry, if you could find the original one for that date? Could you just let me have it for a moment? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour I just wanted to check. The stamp is as smudged on the original as on the photocopy. Your Honour just checking if there is anything I need to ask. I don't think that there is. No, Your Honour, apart from say asking you, sir, that's obviously as we can see one of the documents you provided?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. You can hand that back. Can you now be handed, please, the one dated the 3rd of June, 32/92? Which will be P1869. Again, sir, can you just confirm that's one of the documents that you were given and that you provided to us?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Although unfortunately, it was not photocopied properly in the top corner, but I can see the traces and I know that this is the next, chronologically speaking, document in my records.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, this is the 3rd of June and it says this, the agenda, discussing the conclusions of the Autonomous Region Krajina Crisis Staff in Banja Luka. We look at what was discussed. Mr. Latinovic read the conclusions of the Krajina staff -- Krajina Crisis Staff in Banja Luka reached at the session held on the 29th of the 5th and after discussion the Crisis Staff of the Petrovac municipality gave a proposition for the aforementioned conclusion to be adopted in full. Been decided that all Muslims and Croats who so wish be enabled to evacuate from the territory of the autonomous region, et cetera, et cetera, and effectively it quotes the decision. Then --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Your Honour -- Your Honours may recall that that's one of the ones we have gone through in the gazettes before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In reaching this kind of decision based on the principle of family for family the Autonomous Region of Krajina Crisis Staff bore in mind first of all the fact that several thousand Muslims from Prijedor, Sanski Most and Bosanski Novi in their own free will wish to evacuate to central Bosnia and vice versa. At the same time, the Crisis Staff has decided to confront all the forms of forceful evacuation of the population or evacuation of the population under any kind of pressure and to prevent such attempts with all means possible. And has invited the leaderships of the SDA and HDZ to deal with this. And it deals with that. Now, I just want to jump ahead for a moment and just -- but answer this simply, if you can, yes or no. Here, it's the Crisis Staff of Petrovac has decided that they don't want to forcibly evacuate the population or put any pressure on them. In respect of Petrovac, was that intention actually carried out? In other words, were the people who left doing so without pressure or without any force being applied?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: No. I believe that this is not accurate. People did not leave Bosanski Petrovac voluntarily.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And in fact, it decided to form a board for the implementation of the conclusion of evacuation of Muslims. All right. Thank you. That's that one. Then the next document is --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour in fact there is a note in the diary but -- that relates to a document another one from the 3rd of June which talks about talks with Dr. Karadzic and Mladic but I don't think I need to do that. Actually I think do I. I'm sorry, Your Honour. Could the witness now be handed the notebook? Because there is a couple of things I want to ask. Could Your Honours go to page 8? It's the entry relating to the minutes of 3rd of June, 35/92. I've got them, sorry. Your Honour I do apologise. We have got the minutes. So I'm sorry. It's the next set of minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, you can hand that back to the usher and you'll be handed the proper minutes, it's the 4th of June relating to the 3rd. That's the thing. The agenda for this meeting was the political security station in the municipality -- situation in the municipality and the incident in Biscani. We can see that Mr. Novakovic had had talks with Dr. Karadzic and General Mladic but I want to come to the incident in Biscani, please, which we will find -- it's the third page of our translation. It's under the conclusions, please. Now, first of all, what is Biscani?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Biscani is one part of Bosanski Petrovac inhabited exclusively by Bosniaks or Muslims, and most of the Muslims who were residents of Bosanski Petrovac resided in that particular area.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And do you know what incident this is referring to?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I know exactly what this is all about. This was the first murder that happened in Bosanski Petrovac municipality on the 2nd of June, 1992. Actually it was two murders that took place and a few people were injured, and on that particular evening, there was a lot more shooting than on any other given night.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And here it is said that perpetrators were the conscripts and that the military command was responsible for it. He suggests the military police be responsible for the reservists and the SJB for civilians. All right. Thank you. That should be P1870, please. Can you look now, please, at your next document, 36/92, dated the 5th of June? And I'd just like you to identify again please your writing on the document and then we can leave that.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is my writing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour that is P1871. And then please the next document is the 8th of June, 40/92. And could you just identify again your writing on the document? And that's all we need to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that will be P1 --

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then the next one you brought for us is the 9th of June, 43/92. Could you again please just identify your writing?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. Again, this is my handwriting.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's that one. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: P1873. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
