utterances.text: And we may as well finish them off although we now jump. There is one -- yes, the next one, there is one intervening, Your Honour, which we have already exhibited as P236 so I'm just going to produce these. Could you be handed 10th of June, document which is 50/92? And just again identify your handwriting?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour that will be P -- sorry, Your Honour, what I was saying, I'm sorry, I may have confused something because I rather muttered my way through that. This is the 10th of June and it's got the number 50/92. If Your Honours look at the Petrovac bundle behind number 25, there is one for the 10th of June which bears an earlier number. That's what I was saying. But I think we still go on with the numbers we have got so it's P1874. Your Honour if I'm going too fast for the Registrar, perhaps she can stop me. The next one we've got -- just a moment. Yes, interestingly enough, the number is different but Your Honour it's supposedly dated the 12th of June -- no, I think -- just a moment. Your Honour, that is right. Anyhow it's the 12th of June but it's 48/92.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yours, again, is it, Mr. Hidic?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: P1875. And can we now look, please, at the minutes for the 13th of June, which bear the designation 54/92?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And again, sir, can you confirm that your writing is on the original of this document?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Item number 2 of the decisions -- I'm sorry, yeah, a report -- if we can look at that, a report on the security station was submitted by Mr. Gacesa, the police officer that we saw, and then followed up by Mr. Vrzina. I think you said that he was the TO and Major Radulovic, some negligence, which did however -- however did not seriously affect the security situation, disarmament of the paramilitary formations of -- and citizens who are in illegal possession of arms is to be continued and brought to a close. And then over the page for us, the bodies in charge are to finalise activities regarding the disarmament of the paramilitary formations and citizens who illegally possess weapons. Appropriate repressive measures are to be taken against individuals who took part in illegal armament of paramilitary organisations, et cetera. Now, this is the middle of June or thereabouts. So even after the deadline, was there still disarming orders being given or actions being taken to disarm?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I see that they dealt with this issue, but I really can't give you any specific answers. I don't know whether at this time they were dealing with the issue of disarming and who it was that they were disarming.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's P1876. And then the final two sections, two lots of minutes, both for the 16th of June -- sorry, it's not two. I think it's one. Or was it two? No, that's right. There are two copies of the same set of minutes but there is a difference as we'll see. Can you be handed both, please, for the 16th of June which don't have a number to them?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, are you looking, please, Mr. Hidic, at the ones they have got a number stamped on top, 02930178 and 179?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I have the first one but I don't know -- I don't have the second one. I have --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Have you got two pages with numbers 02930178 and 179?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I do have both. I apologise. I did not see the second page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's got 7 signatures at the end of it; is that right?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now could you have a look, please, at the same document but with the numbers 02930180 and 181? Again, seven signatures; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I don't know whether you can read the signature on number 7, I would be very surprised if you can. But equally, Your Honours, the reason that it appears --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They are different.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: There are different signatures without being handwriting experts that would appear to be the case. So, Your Honour, now I suppose we better have them as the same exhibit number, P1877. Could the higher range, as it were, the 178, 179, copies be point 1 and the second set, point 2? And this is the session held on the 16th of June, and the agenda. And then we see that the President briefly stated the situation on the front and said that our losses included one dead and 19 wounded and he added that he was expecting the Crisis Staff to take a clear stand towards the Muslims while the military post was demanding steps against them to prevent their operative actions and organisation in the rear of our forces. And then it talks about apparently a list of 40 persons believed to be organisers as a special group and paramilitaries and so on and disarmament. I think I asked you earlier today, Mr. Hidic, were you aware, leaving aside people would were actually fighting on the battlefield, were you aware of any armed groups of Muslims operating within Bosanski Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Those are the minutes that you brought with you. Can I just deal with your final three documents then and get that out of the way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The final three documents I take it were the ones which were distributed this morning?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. The one -- they were in the package that Your Honours got. There are three slightly separate documents and Your Honour will recall I said yesterday that, or whatever it was, that there were three documents that we haven't seen before.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The first document, please, will be this -- something headed the Bosanski Petrovac country club report on the events in Bosanski Petrovac. Can you just look at that, please? I'm not sure that the translation is a very good one. Could you just read out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cunningham?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting. Your Honour, has this exhibit been admitted yet?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not yet, no. It's going to be tendered, I suppose together with the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Is it proper to make an objection at this point or should I wait until then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usually if you want to register your an objection you can register it now. It would help us decide if there is a real problem indeed with the admission of this document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It might help, Mr. Cunningham if I ask some questions to establish what it is, how he got it, and what the contents and that might help decide if the objection is based on it's not his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Then in that respect I'm going to go ahead yield the floor at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't have an idea as to what your objection is and I don't have an idea what you are about to ask in any case so do proceed Ms. Korner and then we will take it. You can rest assured, Mr. Cunningham and Mrs. Baruch that the practice we adopt is we are sure there is no prejudice in any case even if a document -- this is why I tell you please do keep in mind all the time that this is a trial being conducted by three professional judges and not -- in the absence of a lay jury. It makes a big difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, could you just read the top line of this document? Just read it out? I want to have the translation.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: The Bosanski Petrovac expatriates club. If that is what you had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is. I didn't think country club was quite --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In fact I was going to ask. Usually I go and play golf in the country club in my country so --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The interpreter yesterday raised her eyebrows when she saw this. As I said, Your Honour, occasionally when you ask for quick interpretation. So expatriate sounds much better.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mr. Hidic, can you just tell us, please, what is this organisation?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: This organisation was established once Bosniaks were expelled from Bosanski Petrovac, and once some of them arrived in Croatia where they were accommodating during the year 1992. And then in late 1992, and early 1993, they established this expatriate's club which was based in Zagreb. Their task according to the information I had, was to establish contacts with everybody from Petrovac who was residing on the territory of Croatia at that time. It was a humanitarian organisation whose aim was to help and assist all the citizens of Bosanski Petrovac who found themselves on the territory of Croatia at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. The report doesn't have a date on it. Do you know when it was actually written?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I believe that it was to mark the first anniversary of the expulsion of Bosniaks from Bosanski Petrovac. There was some sort of a festivity or some sort of a day organised to mark that anniversary and that's the information I had, and it was some year or year and a half after, after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And how did you acquire a copy of this?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: This copy was given to me personally by one of the members of that club. His name was Mase Druzic, if that is something you need to know. He was a member of this club.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, it describes in brief the events that took place in Petrovac from June until the departure in August. Have you read through that, this document?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. I am familiar with this document. I've read it more than once.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is this -- are the descriptions of those events that you know about, are they an accurate description?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I believe that this is a very accurate description of all the developments that took place during the period described in this document, and everything that was happening at that time during the negotiations. If you will allow me I'd like to say that this document also speaks about the members of the forum in Bosanski Petrovac who were in charge of certain activities in Bosanski Petrovac and later on became members of this club.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I think we can see that on the second page.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know Mr. Cunningham wishes to maintain the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Cunningham?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: Judge, I understand the Tribunal's Rules that you can have hearsay on hearsay on hearsay but having said that I'm still going to object to the authenticity of the document, to the extent that there has been what I'll call a lack of corroboration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. That goes on record.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I take it the gentleman you said who gave you this copy himself, you gave us, Mr. Druzic, is he still alive and well?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes. And he lives in Bosanski Petrovac.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. So if it's really necessary and the Defence actually request it, he can come to court and testify that this document was prepared by this club based on the knowledge of the events from the members of this club. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That was a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It was a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: He would be able to come and testify would it, about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Maybe you're expecting a little bit too much from the witness to answer for the other gentleman, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let me put it this way, I'm making a point through the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. The document is being admitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: P1878, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On the face of it. And of course without prejudice to any probative value, if at all, that it might have. This would be P?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 1878. The last two documents, please, that you brought, the first is a communication to the Krajina autonomous region from the Petrovac municipal assembly, sorry, the Petrovac -- Crisis Staff, with the number KS 65/92. Now, Your Honours, I think we better put it up on the ELMO because it refers to a particular decision of the Crisis Staff of the autonomous region. It's Exhibit P255. If we can put that on the ELMO so you can see what it's responding to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This is KS 65/92, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It is, and this document, because it says "Crisis Staff decision number 03531/92" and you can see that at the top of Exhibit 255.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think we need read through it to save time. It's responding to what they were ordered to do and what they've done. The steps envisaged in item 1, para 1, have been implemented, same steps in social owned enterprises, all members of police of Muslim active and reserve sacked, employees of Muslim nationality and the steps by the Krajina Crisis Staff and the stages of being implemented in the BiH Serb republic armies units and blah blah blah. I always wonder how you translate "blah blah blah" but never mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, is this a document that was handed to you or from the municipal assembly building, from the assembly building, in Petrovac?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may that then be made, please, P1880?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And the last document, please, then, which is a communication to Mr. Zupljanin. It's KS 64/92. And it's clearly a report to Mr. Zupljanin from the Crisis Staff signed by Mr. Novakovic, stamped, again is that a document that you were given apparently originating from the municipal building?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Your Honours, that is Exhibit P1880. And those are all the new documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With regard to this document, Ms. Korner, sir, can I ask you to read to yourself the last main paragraph starting, "Due to insufficient training or excessive tolerance."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, that thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Read it out because then I'm going to ask you a question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You'd like me to read it out, yes. It says here, sir, that due to insufficient training or excessive tolerance, at present in our town, just like in all other small towns, members of our police have not been able to put an end to it. That's mass theft, I think it's referring to. Well, it says -- Your Honour I think we need to go to the paragraph before. It says we are also witnessing mass theft in areas where combat or cleansing operations are taking place or have already taken place. Then it talks about the training and tolerance, and then says we are asking you to immediately send one special purpose police detachment to Petrovac to bring peace and prevent the decreasing morale among part of our population, including members of the Serbian army, and to prevent anarchy and chaos.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Taking you back to that period in time, Mr. Hidic, did you notice any difference -- first of all, would you accept that the description being given by Rajko Novakovic in this memo to Stojan Zupljanin is a true picture of the situation in the area at the time? Would you agree that it was so, that there was mass theft and that during police curfew, there was shooting, demolishing and looting of taverns, shops, even of Serbs? Would you accept that that was taking place around about the last week of June of the year 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely. I would agree with what is stated here. Your Honours, with your permission I would like to corroborate this with facts. At the time, a large number of cars that had been stolen and were in Bosanski Petrovac municipality, driven by soldiers and various other people, so perhaps this fact is something that prompted them into writing this. I know that there was a lot of looting going on and that items that had been stolen were confiscated, and these items were found in certain areas where Serb soldiers were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And in the subsequent weeks and perhaps months but not too many, did you notice any change for the better or did things remain the same or get worse? After the 25th of June, 1992, after the end of June, 1992, in other words. Was there a change in the state of affairs that you've just described?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that there had been some changes. In fact, I know that there were certain forces, I don't know if they were regular police or military police, going around and confiscating what the members of the Serb army called as war booty, so various looted items, and all of that was stored in front of the police station. So I can tell you that effort was made in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And would you know where these policemen that restored a little bit of order came from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I truly don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But were they from your area, from the municipality, or from outside the municipality?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Ms. Korner. Judge Janu would like to put an additional question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: When you say it was confiscated, what do you mean by that? It was written back to the owners or it was confiscated by the municipality -- it belonged to the municipality

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. It was not returned. It was stored on the grounds of the police administration in Bosanski Petrovac. Some of the items were stored there. So it was -- it was confiscated from some of the people, not from all of the people. And this is why I said that there were some changes and that perhaps was put into force because of this appeal written appeal, that was issued previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: So there was no any attempt to give it back to the owners, those cars and other items?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know of a single case where it was returned to its rightful owner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Korner?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, can I just ask two questions on that document, please, while you've still got it, sir? First, it refers to areas which have been cleansed. By June of -- 25th of June, were there any cleansing operations taking place? In other words, expulsions? That you knew of?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: If I can say so, I think that this pertains to certain areas where members of the Serb army were already present, at least that's how I understand it, that this refers to those very areas that were already occupied by the Serb army. In Bihac area, in Kulen Vakuf, in Orasac and so on, perhaps even Bosanska Krupa.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. And secondly, it says, please send a special purpose police detachment. To your knowledge, was -- did such -- was such a police detachment ever sent?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I have a piece of information, and I'm now referring to the same source, that an officer, Atlagic, was appointed, and his task was to attempt to resolve these issues of looted property through military police or rather to confiscate it from the person in whose possession the looted item was.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. You say from your source. Now, we've looked at a number of the Crisis Staff decisions you acquired after 1995 or after the war was over. At the time, in 1992, through May and June, were you, the Bosniaks, being told -- not obviously word for word, but what was happening in these Crisis Staff meetings?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: It was impossible to know what was going on there. Not directly. We had no direct knowledge of what was going on. We had no access to such places. We couldn't even access the building of municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You've -- you said you had a source who told you about this police officer being appointed and you said there were still contacts between Serbs and the Bosniaks. Were you being given any information about what was being planned for Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Naturally, it was a public secret in Bosanski Petrovac that Muslims from that town would never be able to go to Bihac, but that they would rather be directed towards central Bosnia. It was a public secret. It was already prepared, the road that they would have to take, although different things were said in public. If I understood your question correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Now, there are just three other documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours I didn't put them on the list because it's only now that I've appreciated the difference. If Your Honours and the Defence please look at P245, which is a Crisis Staff minute for the 14th of June, number 55/92? And Your Honours, Mr. Hidic provided attached to his second statement what I thought was an identical copy. It is if you look at the English but it's not if you look at his copy. I think he better have a look, please, at the attachment, not P245, please, but the attachment to his statement. It's got the number 7.61 on it. Okay. I'm sorry, in that case, we've got another copy. I think Your Honours have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can the witness -- I don't think we gave it -- we didn't put it on the list for the Registry, so...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have one, 245 but.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You didn't get it either. I'm sorry, Your Honours. In that case, can I exhibit it formally through him and I'll make sure that everybody has copies but the Defence -- I know it wasn't on the list it would have been an attachment to the second statement but we will make more copies.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: First of all, sir, can you identify that as one of the documents that you received from the municipal assembly documents? A photocopy of it, rather? With your writing in the right-hand side?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can you just put it on the ELMO so that Their Honours and -- could we move it so that the right-hand corner -- yeah. And then could we now put it on the last page of that document, on to the ELMO? And if Your Honours look at 245 in the last page, there is a difference. I'm sorry, can I just see what you're putting up? That should be -- I'm sorry, it should be -- I think this is a mistake here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's a different one, no?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's a different one but it does actually correspond with another document which is P -- no, no, hang on one minute. Sorry. I think I'll leave that until Monday, put the two bundles together because I only spotted it now and I think I'm going to confuse the issue horribly. We will deal with this Monday and I'll move on. It's my fault.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Can we then, please, now, move --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, did Your Honour say 4 or 4.30?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 4.00 but if we need to stay up to 4.30, I have no problems if the other two Judges and the rest of you -- pardon? We have to take into consideration, exactly, the interpreters the technicians.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's what I'm asking because we have gone for an hour and three-quarters already without a break and if we were, I was simply going to say I imagine there has to be a change of tapes anyhow, don't we have to change them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We will soon know.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We have a two hour tape so we can go to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let us go up to 4.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That was agreed beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So then can we then, please, just, I think, move through what happened in the major months really of June, July and August? And I think perhaps the best way of dealing with this is if you go back to the Croatian list of events and fill in what you know about these. And if I have my own copy. I've forgotten what the exhibit number is. It's this one. The country club. It's Exhibit P1878. There we see the events that they say, the first arrests started in Petrovac on the 13th of June, and then on the 18th of June, the killing of the people from -- called Kavaz. Now, did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: When did you first hear about it?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: That same day. It took place in the evening and the very next day I knew about the killing of the Kavaz couple. So I knew about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If we move then to July the 3rd, we see there that Muslims who had been detained at the police station were taken to the Kozila camp. Now you told us about the police station and you said that there was another camp. When was the first time that you heard about this camp?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: The first time was when the -- when the people who had been arrested and interrogated at the police station were taken there. Their wives, their family members, already knew about that, and they attempted to make contact with them and to take some clothing and other items to them. I believe that they insisted upon that on a daily basis. They pleaded with Rajko Novakovic, with Serb authorities. They waited in front of the municipality for days in order to see them and to pass on their requests.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Did you yourself know that a camp had been established in Kozila? I'm sorry, did you know anybody who had been taken to that camp, is the proper question.

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: I knew almost all of the people who were imprisoned. Some I knew directly. Some people were my relatives, distant relatives, close relatives, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Now, can you look, please, at Exhibit P1838? This is a session of the Crisis Staff on the 30th of June?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On the 29th.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, yes, it's the date of the document that is the 30th. It was held on the 29th, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Mr. Novakovic is dealing with the political and security situation and then if you look at the second paragraph, the Muslims of Petrovac are behaving as if they are wounded and are showing great fear. More of them should be arrested and isolated as a precaution. After which they should be given work obligations because there will be a lot of harvesting to do. First, would you agree with that assessment, that the Muslims in Petrovac were showing great fear?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Definitely. They lived in constant fear, which was especially obvious in the evening hours, or rather during curfew, and this fear brought people together, in fact. They met with other people in order not to be alone. Complete absolute fear reigned among them. All of us could feel that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you aware of people being arrested and isolated as a precaution, in other words not having committed an offence, and then being sent off to do harvesting?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: These people who had been isolated and imprisoned were not sent to do that but rather other people were called up, mobilised, to do those kind of tasks. I myself received summons to do that and participated in one such activity.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And then can we go to the conclusion number 1 of that document? Until the prison in Kozila -- I think that should read Kozila rather than -- maybe -- is made operational, a plan should be made to arrest and bring in under custody all Muslims fit for military service who are thought to be capable of causing any harm to the Serbs. Was that something that happened? Men of military age were just arrested?

utterances.speaker: AHMET HIDIC
utterances.text: Definitely. They were not just imprisoned but during those days, they -- those who were not imprisoned had to report to the police administration twice a day, in the morning and in the evening, not just men but also women who were treated just like men, they also had to report twice, once in the morning and once in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours in fact I'm going to move on to the topic of the murders and expulsions so that's probably appropriate. Your Honour, I anticipate I should be one -- just another hour on Monday morning. With a bit of optimism.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you anticipate, Mr. Cunningham, that you will be in a position to conclude your cross on Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. CUNNINGHAM
utterances.text: My hope is that my cross will be long enough to cover the subject but short enough to be interesting. I think I will be done by the end of the day, easily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So perhaps you can make arrangements, Ms. Korner, for the return of --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I explained to Mr. Hidic yesterday that he'd have to now wait until Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Ms. Korner and thank you, Mr. Hidic, for understanding. So the case stands adjourned until Monday, 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that will be an extended-hours day. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
